speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs

speechtext: The rule of Parliament refers to twenty days. This matter has been allowed to go on for nearly four years before this question was raised.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is true, but because this motion could have been made
with much less force three years ago, is that a reason why it should not be made now? If the rules of the House are being defied by a member sitting for two seats for a month, is it not infinitely worse that he should sit for two seats for three years?
By prescriptive right.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I hear my hon. friend say that he has now got a prescriptive right, just as a man might have to a piece of land by remaining on it for ten years.

Is my right hon. friend
aware from his reading of Bourinot, that Bourinot declares that rule 79 has been honoured more in the breech than in the observance ever since it has been on the book?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I may have read that, but I never heard that seriously put forward as a reason for continuing to defy the rule, much less as a reason for evading it.
I only wanted to know if my right hon. friend was aware of that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I had not read that
statement in Bourinot, but I have read in Bourinot that when any question arises respecting the seat of a member, it is the custom for the hon. member affected immediately to state his case and withdraw. I have read that in Bourinot. I was not going to press that, but that is the point which came to my notice first when I looked up Bourinot on this question. I do not wish to press it though. The case is also covered by rule 69 of our own book applicable to this House. Anyway, the question is this:	whether this House can logically
resist a motion which sets out that a rule of this House is being evaded by a fictitious proceeding in the courts. Undoubtedly, if the court had jurisdiction, if it were the duty of the court without an application by either side to put an end to this farce, if it is a farce, why then it would be for the courts to do it; but if the courts have not done so, is it not the duty of this House to see that its rules are carried out? Can this House logically resist a motion made to see that its rules are adhered to, that the facts be investigated; first of all to ascertain whether there is an evasion or violation of the rules, and then, if it turn out that there is, to see that the rules are put into execution? I do not see how the motion can be resisted.
I hope I have at least made it clear to hon. members of this House that this is

not a case of a controverted election and a request to decide it in Parliament. If it were, I would not be found in support of the motion. This is not such a case at all. This is not a case of the House seeking to decide something that the courts have been given jurisdiction to decide. This is a case of the House being called upon to support and stand by its own rules, and inquire whether or not they are being evaded, and evaded in such a way that the courts cannot stop it; that we alone can stop it.

Is it not competent for any person to appear before the courts and argue along the line my right hon. friend is arguing, that the case is fictitious, and have it disposed of by the courts instead of by a partisan committee?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Where I practised law, in the province of Manitoba, the only man who could appear in a case was a party to the case; he could be added as a third party.
He can in Quebec.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Can appear and be heard in argument to show that both parties are merely fictitious parties and that there in no real case? I have never practised in the province of Quebec, but I venture to doubt that.
It is the federal law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Who would assert that it is the duty of any of the parties to the action to go there and, because some one could, if perchance he can, which I very much doubt, say that this House should sit idly by and wait till somebody takes a notion to go ahead and get in between the two parties to the ligitation and say they are both fictitious. I would not like to be found resisting the motion on that ground.
What I assert is this. There is a prima facie ease. The hon. member for Fron-tenac has established it. What do you need to establish a prima facie case that there is no real contention as to the validity of the allegation, more than the fact that the petition is now nearly three-and-a-half years old, and the petitioner has not even suggested the putting forward of a tittle of evidence to support his allegation. After three-and-a-half years, while the law calls, first, for thirty days, not a tittle of evidence has been presented in support of his allegations. That, to my mind, establishes a prima facie case at once. Secondly, if as is alleged by the hon. member, the petitioner is a friend and supporter of the
[Mr. Meighen. 3
member elected, that would seem to me to add circumstantial evidence in support of the allegation. Thirdly, after some two or three years that the petition had lain dead there in the courts, and when it appeared that there would be at least doubt as to whether the law of the land did not automatically declare that it was dead without the intervention of anybody the respondent himself comes in and says: I want to change my lawyers; I do not want this petition dismissed; I do not say that the petitioner has gone out to Manitoba or Alberta; I am not asking to dismiss this petition that has lain dormant for nearly three years, but I would like to change my lawyers; the men I have had have become so exhausted sitting up nights working on this case for three years that they cannot stand it any longer, and I will have to have another set of lawyers to protect me in this fierce and arduous ligitation. So he launches a motion that the firm of coun sel be changed, and I suppose that by reason of that change some further time would be given him in order to get ready his defence against this most dangerous assailant. That would look to me to be very circumstantial and rather forceful evidence in support of the assumption that the whole thing was fictitious from the beginning, intended as an evasion of the rules of the House, intended, indeed, as a contempt of the high court of Parliament. That is what is alleged by the hon. member for Frontenac. Why should he not have permission to establish that, if he can, before the Committee on Privileges and Elections? What is the Committee on Privileges and Elections for? It is not to try controverted elections; we all know that. Can anybody suggest something that the Privileges and Elections Committee can do if this work is to be denied them?

Give a seat to the
member for Yukon Territory, as it did two years ago.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That was a case precisely similar to this, and the committee acted. Why should it not act now? I know the hon. gentleman was anxious, and many more who were in association with hin were anxious, that votes cast in France-
Wave the flag.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -by the soldiers should not be counted in that contest because they would elect the present hon. member for Yukon.
Shame.
Cheap.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is the ground
upon which he makes the assertion now. I know it is altogether aside from the argument-
Wave the flag.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Hon. members opposite are much more eloquent in their seats, when they cannot very well be heard, than when they get on their feet. .
I said, wave the flag.
I said, shame.
I said, cheap.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. member has properly described himself, so I do not see why I should object.
That applies to your work.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. gentleman surely knows the rule that he is not in order in making remarks from his seat while another hon. member is speaking. The only privilege he has in that respect is to ask a question, with the consent of the hon. member addressing the House.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for Frontenac has made certain statements which so far have not been disputed. The first fact which he has given-that is, what he states to be the fact, and it is not so far disputed-is that a petition was lodged and has lain since shortly after the election until this day without any prosecution whatsoever, without any action to refute the allegation that it is evasive and fictitious. He has given further a statement, which so far I have not heard disputed, if it has been: that the petitioner himself was a supporter of the hon. member and a personal friend of his. This is alleged by the hon. member for Frontenac, and whether it is subsequently disputed or not it constitutes an allegation in support of the charge he makes. The third is that so far from seeking to have this petition disposed of, as might be expected to be the conduct of a respondent, the conduct of the respondent has been consistent rather with the desire on his part to have the petition lie there and perform the service that it is performing now. All these things he has alleged.
If they are true, they undoubt-5 p.m. edly constitute an evasion of the rule of this House, an evasion that does not make it the duty of the courts, apart from the motion of either
party-unless some third party happens to come in, and his power to come in I doubt-to put an end to that sort of proceeding. Therefore I say that these constitute facts which, as they do build a case for evasion, make it impossible for this House to resist an inquiry on the part of an appropriate committee. I submit, therefore, with all deference, that it is the duty of the House to support the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be
very brief in my remarks. I wish at once to relieve the mind of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) in connection with his intimation that I should have made a statement at once with regard to this matter and withdraw from the House.
I do not read the rules as my right hon. friend does. Rule 69 says:
If anything shall come In question touching the return or election of any member, he is to withdraw during the time the matter is in debate; and all members returned upon double returns are to withdraw until their returns are determined.
I do not see anything in that rule which would apply in my case as it has been presented to the House this afternoon.
The motion, Mr. Speaker, is a strange one. Is it a charge? The right hon. gentleman a moment ago, referring to the hon. member for Frontenac, used the word "charge." If it is a charge brought against the member for Maisonneuve, the right hon. gentleman knows that there is a proceeding to follow in that regard. If a charge were made against the right hon. gentleman or against the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) or against the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) the member preferring the charge should be ready in that case to put his seat in jeopardy. But I do not take his motion as a charge. True, there is a vague innuendo in the speech delivered by the member for Frontenac, but there is no charge in the motion. If there was, I would ask you, Mr. Speaker, to apply the well-known rule that no member may prefer a charge against a fellow member without putting his seat in jeopardy in the substantiation of that charge.
I have nothing to complain of so far as the remarks made by the hon. member for Frontenac are concerned. It strikes me, however, that in this matter there is one system of justice for the minority and another for the majority. My right hon. friend the Minister of Justice waxed very eloquent as to the

impropriety of a member evading the law, trampling on the rules of the House by not electing within the specified time for one of the two seats for which he has been elected. I will put a question straight to my right hon. friend. He was on the Bench for nearly twenty years; he is now the Minister of Justice and custodian of at least the Dominion law. He was the Minister of Justice, sworn in as such in 1911, and he sat for six years in the possession of that portfolio and as a member of the House of Commons in Canada. One of his followers, was my late friend and opponent the then member for Charlevoix and Montmorency. Does not the right hon. gentleman know that no protest was lodged against the return of the late Sir Rodolphe Forget? Does he not know that that hon. gentleman sat during six years for both constituencies next to him in the House, and never was the eloquent voice of the right hon. gentleman raised in protest against the presence in the House of the late Sir Rodolphe Forget? Two-ways, Mr. Speaker, of administering justice as understood by the right hon. gentleman.
Now, I will put another question to the right hon. gentleman, because he used the word "fraud." Sir, I resent that expression falling from the lips of the Minister of Justice. No man has ever traduced me; no man has ever accused me of having committed a fraud or participated in a fraudulent act, and I will not allow any man to do so. If it is fraud for the member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe to occupy two seats in the House, is it fraud for a right hon. gentleman whom I am told has affixed his signature to a document settling a number of Dominion election protests? If that is a fact, surely it was a fraud, and it would have been a criminal act. I heard of a certain right hon. gentleman who did that. I lay no charge, but the right hon. gentleman will not with impunity use the word "fraud" with reference to me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman desire an answer to his question? If the hon. gentleman had followed what I said I think he would have perceived that I did not charge him with fraud; that what I,said was that the statements that were made prima facie indicated, gave ground for, belief that there was fraud, and called for inquiry. I was careful throughout my speech, and if I did not succeed in making that clear, I am sorry, I strove to do it-	.

Does my right hon.
friend withdraw the word "fraud?"

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I wish to state that I did not charge the hon. gentleman with fraud, nor with anything else.
Thank you.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may say that I tried to make that clear; but what I sought to put before the House was that, upon the facts as presented to the House, there was a case for inquiry. As the hon. gentleman will remember, I pointed out that I thought that was due, in justice to this House and, in particular, to himself.

I thank the right hon. gentleman for his explanation, but I did not like the imputation of fraud which I read through his remarks. I accept the explanation that he has given to me and to the House. Once more, I resent such an insinuation, as I have never been charged with fraud, and I hope to live and die without any such imputation being brought against me.
The right hon. gentleman said a moment ago that he understood, by the motion made by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards), that, first, the petitioner was a friend of mine. I declare upon my word of honour that I do not personally know the petitioner who had that petition served upon me. In fact, I am almost certain that he was an opponent of mine. Second, I am not aware that he has disappeared, as was slightly hinted by the hon. member for Frontenac. Third, as it was suggested that some of the documents had disappeared from the record, my answer is that I have seen the record for the first time this morning. I wrote to my attorneys in Montreal for it, and I hold it in my hand. If there are any papers missing from the original record, I have in my private record, copies of all those documents, and I shall be pleased, whenever I am asked, to give duplicates either to the committee or to the Superior Court in Montreal. But, perhaps, the hon. gentleman may have thought that there was some suspicion of a disappearance of documents because, as a matter of fact, there are very few documents in that record. There is the petition; there is my appearance, and there are two or three motions made. That is all.
I wish to say to the House that what I said in 1919, I abide by. I am firmly convinced that it is not sound practice that a member should be returned for two seats.
I came to that conclusion long ago.
Oh, oh.

It is a custom which has been followed in the past on both sides of the House-I hear laughter on the other side-it is a custom which was followed by Sir John A. Macdonald. It has been followed, I believe, by the ex-Prime Minister of Canada (Sir Robert Borden). It has been followed by the late Sir Rodolphe Forget, and by many other hon. gentlemen from the other party, since Confederation. It has also been followed by some hon. members of the Liberal party. But I repeat what I said in 1919. We live in a more democratic era and this practise is undemocratic. At the earliest opportunity, when my hands are legally free, I intend to avail myself of the stand I took in 1919. I supported in this House the reform advocated by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs), and my sincerity need not be questioned. If a gentleman is sometimes elected for two constituencies, I am human enough to admit that that is due to party exigencies. All the more fortunate for him if he is elected; yet everybody knows that if it is quite a task to represent one constituency, to represent two constituencies is certainly no sinecure.
I wish at once to correct a statement made by the hon. member for Frontenac a moment ago. He said that I was elected in 1904 for the constituencies of Nicolet and Gaspe. That is true. He said that it took me one or two sessions before I made the statutory declaration. That is true. But I was protested.

I accepted my hon.
friend's statement at the time.

I want to emphasize
the fact. I was protested, if I mistake not, by my opponent, Mr. Ball, who for a number of years was member for the constituency of Nicolet. It was only when a judgment of the court dismissed the petition against me that I was in a position, in the early part of the session of 1906, to declare that I elected for the constituency of Gaspe, and then the late Hon. Charles Devlin was elected in the constituency of Nicolet.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) found it strange that so many months had elapsed without any move being taken in the matter. Of course, it would strike popular imagination that, indeed, the process of law was long. It would strike any one that it should have lasted so long,
and, perhaps, some might suggest that the parties in the case are not averse to prolonging the delays.
Hear, hear.
Who says, hear, hear?
I was the guilty party.

I absolve the hon. gentleman. I thought it was my good friend the hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer). Let me call the attention of the House to one or two circumstances. The last election took place in 1917; a certain delay elapsed, and a protest was served upon me just prior to the session of 1918. Hon. gentlemen know that all proceedings are stayed during the session, which was a fairly long one. * After the session was over, it happened that the legal holidays were in progress, and no procedure took place. Is there anything very strange in that?-I appeal to my hon. friends, who belong to the legal profession. There is nothing anomalous in that. Then the session of 1919 began, and I was present at that session for only a few days. I leave it to the House to say whether or not, because I had to leave for France early in that session and that I remained away for nearly seven months, I made that trip to evade any legal process. I was away the greater part of the year. I came back towards the end of last session, and then again there-were the legal holidays, so therefore-
Oh, oh.

Who laughs? Is that
true, or is it not? I say that as soon as last session was prorogued, there was the legal holidays. I remained outside of this country for several months, it is true, but no one in this House will dare to say that it was to evade any process of law in the courts of this country. Now, Mr. Speaker, the rule of the House is:
All members who are returned for two or more electoral districts shall make their election for which of the districts they will serve within twenty days after it shall appear that there is no question upon the return for either district.
I am ready to leave this matter to the courts of the land. I am a King's Counsel. In my professional career I have never played any tricks; I have never acted the sharp practitioner before any of the courts of this land. I repudiate with all my might any innuendo or insinuation against

my good faith in this matter, and the best evidence of my good faith, Mr. Speaker, I will give to the House at once.
My hon. friend has made his motion. I could hardly have expected that he would present his case in the manner he did. I expected that he would be less moderate, less judicial, more partisan than he was, because we see eye to eye on hardly any question that comes before the House. But from the right hon. the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) who is thoroughly conscious of all that the word justice implies, who is an old judge, and who knows me, I could have expected language less sarcastic, less persiflage, a tone more judicial. As I have said, he did not choose to adopt that tone whilst speaking of a fellow-member who has occupied a seat in this House for twenty-five years. I do not complain of that; I am accustomed to the rough-and-tumble of public life. But there are certain amenities which should be maintained in public as well as in private life. I thank my hon. friend from Frontenac for the manner in which he has brought this matter before the House. I might have perhaps expected a longer notice from him before bringing this matter up, but he has presented his case in a gentlemanly way, for which I sincerely thank him. I shall have no difficulty whenever the time comes in dispelling from his mind the cloud of suspicion which evidently over-haiigs it. I shall help him in getting all the papers and witnesses and court officials, and will do everything in my power to dispel the opaque cloud of doubt and suspicion which blurs his conscience. I also invite the moderator of the synod of justice, the custodian of the Dominion law, the fair interpreter of the statutes in the spirit and in the letter, to appear before the Committee on Privileges and Elections, and to follow closely my train and see whether I have been acting fraudulently or not. I might perhaps have occasion then to cross-examine my right hon. friend on some of his own election ventures.
I hope that the House will not divide. I do not care to leave the matter any longer in suspense. Let the Committee on Privileges and Elections make this inquiry, and send for all the papers and witnesses it desires. When that committee, Mr. Speaker, has fully inquired into all the facts of this case, it will be found that the hon. member for Gaspe and Maisonneuve is willing and indeed anxious to live up not only to the letter of rule 79, but to its spirit, because it is the very spirit of the British constitu-

tion and of ours that a man should be elected, for~one seat and one seat only.
As the hon. member has mentioned my constituency, may I ask whether according to the practice of his province a respondent can apply to dismiss for want of prosecution?
Yes, certainly.
Can he also apply to speed the case?

Certainly.
Mr. KEEFElt: Has that been done?

No, not in my case. As I have explained, I could not proceed during the session; I could not proceed during the legal holiday; I could not proceed when I was in Europe. But I am ready to proceed immediately the session is over, and I have given instructions accordingly.

I see by the record I have had placed in my hands that the motion for delay on behalf of the respondent, the hon. member for Maisonneuve, was supported by an affidavit. I would like to know who made that affidavit.
I have it here. It bears my name. I made the affidavit myself.
Has the hon member any objection to letting me see it?
None at all. I will send it over now.

Mr. Speaker, I have just one observation to make. I listened with some attention to the remarks made by the right hon. the Prime Minister and I gathered from what he said that he thought there was no possibility of getting rid of collusion, if there happened to be collusion, unless the matter was brought before the Privileges and Elections Committee. I would point out that the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, as found in the statutes of 1906, chapter 7, provides by section 39:
If at the expiration of three months after such petition has been presented, the day for trial has not been fixed, any elector may, on application, be substituted for the petitioner on such terms as the court thinks just.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: For the petitioner.
Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That would not help any.

I understood the argument of my learned and hon. friend to be that the petitioner was a make-believe peti-

tioner, that he was there not for the purpose of proceeding against the respondent, but of preventing other people from proceeding against him. That is my understanding of his argument.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I did not say it was to prevent any one else from proceeding at all. What I argued, or [DOT] rather what the Minister of Justice argued, was that the provision enabling one person to take the place of another who might be a fake petitioner was to enable the petition to proceed and not be dropped. That is not the present case. The present petitioner does not want to have it dropped; he is only too willing to have the matter stand just where it is.

As I understand the objection of hon. members of the other side to this proceeding in Montreal, it is that the court is not functioning, that the proceeding is not proceeding, if I may use that Hibernianism, with apologies to the Minister of Justice. That is what I understand to be the difficulty with my learned and hon. friends opposite. That is a misconception of the law, because if there is any suspicion in the mind of any one in that regard, the Government is able to find one or two friends in Maisonneuve-they must have at least one or two-whom they can get to make application to the court and ask that they be substituted for the petitioner. The question comes to this: whether it is wiser to have judicial questions settled by a court, or by a committee which of necessity must be more or less partisan in its constitution.

I congratulate my hon.
friend from Maisonneuve and Gaspe (Mt. Lemieux), upon the determination which he has reached. It occurred to me in the early stages of the debate that it would have been well for him then to arise and announce the determination which 'I felt sure he would announce in the end. I have therefore nothing to say on the case that has been presented or the answer that has been, given, but I desire to say a word or two on the general question as to the right of this Parliament to deal with matters affecting the status of members of this House. That particular question really does not arise here, but as so much has been said about it, I should like to remind hon. gentlemen that it was very thoroughly discussed in this House upon a motion which I made in 1899 when I brought to the
attention of Parliament, after the time for filing petitions had passed, certain alleged irregularities respecting the return of members of this House for the constituency of West Huron and the constituency of Brockville in the province of Ontario. The motion I made was based on affidavits indicating that at a certain poll in the riding of West Huron, and also at least one poll in the riding of Brockville, more electors had voted for the Conservative candidate in these ridings than was indicated by the number of ballots actually found in the box afterwards. The motion I made was consented to by the then leader of the Government, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who thought that I had made a fairly strong case with respect to West Huron, but rather a weak one with regard to Brockville; and we entered into a long investigation of the question, under the determination of the House so reached with the consent of both parties. So the rule which has been alluded to by several hon. members in this debate has not quite the limitations which have been suggested by some other hon. gentlemen. Now, so far as the real question in this matter is concerned, it is perfectly true that there is within the reach of the judicial authorities in the province of Quebec a method of determining whether or not this petition is collusive. That is the real test of the case put forward by the member for Prontenac. I am not disposed to accept the conclusion that, because it is competent for the courts of that province to reach such a determination in dealing with that question, therefore this House would be utterly helpless if it were plain that the petition was kept alive through collusion. I am not in the least suggesting, as my hon. friend from Maisonneuve will understand, that there was collusion, because I readily appreciate the fact that we must accept the opposite view until the contrary is determined after fair investigation. But I put to hon. members in this House this question: Suppose it were admitted frankly on the floor of the House that a particular petition had been originated or afterwards maintained through collusion, would any hon. member say that this House would be utterly helpless under those circumstances? It could not be pretended for one moment. I am sure the Committee on Privileges and Elections would determine and report to the House that a collusive petition was no petition at all within the meaning of the rule, and that the House would be in a position to take action just

as if no such petition had been originated or maintained. However, that is purely with regard to the principle which the House ought to accept in dealing with a question of this kind. Fortunately, my hon. friend from Maisonneuve has taken what I conceive to be the proper and manly course in this case, and the whole question raised by the member for Frontenac will be under consideration by the Committee on Privileges and Elections.

For a good many years I have followed rather closely the enforcement of our election law, and that law, like many another of our federal laws, falls down because we have no federal enforcement of the statutes we pass in this Parliament. In this country there ought to be a federal enforcement of federal laws, and we are gradually coming to an appreciation of the importance of this. They had to come to it in the United States, and I think that when we have laws on our statute books governing elections to this Parliament, and matters of a similar character, we ought to have a federal court for their enforcement. There has been objection to this from a provincial standpoint, and the question has come up time after time; but I think that the mere fact that we have federal laws governing our elections is sufficient warranty for having a federal court for their enforcement. The right hon. gentleman (Sir Robert Borden), at one stage of his career in this House, had some doubt as to the wisdom of this policy, but I was glad to hear him some years ago declare that he was being impressed more and more by the necessity for this Parliament taking this view of the question, and ultimately seeing to it that the interpretation and enforcement of federal laws, and especially of the law that concerns the election of members of this House, their rights, and the rights of the electors, shall lie with a federal court, where, if there were any unnecessary delay or any attempt at a violation of democratic principles, we could rectify it in this House.

I want to draw the attention of the right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) to the argument which he made in connection with this matter. It is contended that a process, which must be regular and lawful-the filing of the petition-has been used in this case improperly and illegally as a subterfuge and is therefore, an abuse of the process of the court. Now if there

has been an abuse of the process of any court, where ought you to go to have it rectified? You go before that court whose process has been abused. You give notice of motion that you are going to move to strike out the rule of summons, if it is a rule. If it is a petition that has been filed, you move that the petition be struck off the records of the court. That is the proper course to follow and that has not been done in this ease. A petition has been filed, it stands there yet, it is there to-day, and it must therefore be accepted as proper until it is set aside. Rule 79 that we are dealing with is a conditional rule; there is added to it a condition, and while the condition exists the rule does not apply. It is something like talking about the statute of limitations where we say the statute does not run while the man concerned is out of the country. In this case it is a condition to the application of this rule that there should be no impediment to the election or no objection raised to it. The rule of the House is as follows:	*
All members who are returned for two or more electoral districts shall make their election for which of the districts they will serve, within twenty days after it shall appear that there is no question upon the return for either district.
Well, there is a question here. Will the Minister of Justice or the right hon. member for King's, N.S. say that there is not? A petition has been filed questioning the hon. gentleman's right to the seat and that immediately comes within this rule. There is no obligation upon any member who is returned for two seats, to resign or take any steps until that impediment is removed and the case has been heard. If anybody is holding a seat improperly there is a proceeding well known to the warranto, of this country as a writ of quo warranto. My hon. friend from Frontenac, or some lawyer representing him, could go before the Supreme Court of Canada, or a judge of the Supreme Court of Quebec, and move for an order of the court calling upon the hon. member for Maisonneuve to show cause why he was occupying a seat in this House. The hon. member for Maisonneuve then would have to appear before a properly constituted court and make good his position. That is the law. The right hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) smUes.
I smiled, Mr. Speaker, because I never heard before that quo warranto could be used to test the right of a member to sit in Parliament.

If it applies in the case of one public man, where proceedings have been entered in the courts, why should it not apply in the case of another? For example, there is not the slightest difference between the position of a member of Parliament or the position of a member of a municipal council as far as the holding of the seat is concerned. In each case the man is holding office by virtue of an election; he is elected for a certain term and he sits by reason of the course of that election. If you can bring a municipal councillor before the courts to show that he won his seat in that council improperly why cannot you adopt the same procedure in the case of a member of the local Legislature? Let me give an illustration. Supposing the law required that a man should be solvent before he could hold a seat in any legislature of the Dominion? Despite this law a man who has became insolvent nevertheless retains his seat, we will say, in the Legislature of the province of Ontario. Very well, you go before the Supreme Court of that province and summon that man there to show how it is that he, an insolvent, in contravention of the statute, continues to hold the seat. I make that assertion as a common-sense principle in law. That is the way in which you pro*-ceed to attack a man who has been disqualified but is still holding his seat in the Legislature; There is no other way of getting at him so far as I know.
However, I do not wish to wander from the point at issue which is: that while this petition, made in compliance with the law, stands I submit this is not the proper tribunal of the House to decide the matter at issue; the exhibition of partisanship which has been displayed here this afternoon is the best and most conclusive evidence of that. I have always maintained that a partisan parliament-and all parliaments are more or less of that character -is not the judicial, calm and deliberate body which should deal with points of law -the courts are there to decide such questions. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that any person who questions the validity or propriety of this petition should have gone before some judge in the province of Quebec, a proceeding for which there was abundant opportunity, and asked that this petition be dismissed. Once that was done the coast was clear, and if the hon. member for Maisonneuve, my deskmate then continued to occupy his seat in defiance of those proceedings, I would have no fault to find with the Committee on
Privileges and Elections dealing with the case. But while this petition stands we should not make ourselves the judges of what has been done, or is being done, or should be done in the Supreme Court of the province of Quebec. I submit, Sir, that to do as we are asked would be taking a very dangerous step. We should be discharging a duty which should be calmly and deliberately discharged by a judge, and not by a partisan tribunal such as we have in this House.

The debate has lasted a very long time and I have no desire to prolong it. But the hon. member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe having sent me over a copy of the notice of motion in the trial proceedings and of the affidavit supporting it. I think it would be well to put that affidavit on record so as to make the record complete.
I do not believe there is any document missing, but if there is, I shall be only too pleased- to supply it in order to complete the record. I am ready to give all the information that is desired.

This document is in
French. I suppose my hon. friend has no objection to my translating it as I proceed so that it may go upon the record in English.
Not at all; it is a public document.

Province of Quebec, District of Montreal Superior Court No. 12.
Controverted Elections Act.
In -the matter of the election of a member of the House of Commons of Canada for the electoral district of Maisonneuve, in the judicial district of Montreal, held on November 19, and December 17, 1917, being respectively the days for nomination and voting.
Albert Gadboua, petitioner, vs. the Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux, respondent.
Motion for prolongation or continuation of delay.	.
Whereas a petition in contestation of election has been presented in this matter on March 15, 1917, and whereas the respondent desires to make a motion for particulars to reply to the said petition such as prescribed by the law and to take all proceedings that he will judge necessary in time and place.
Whereas the delay for taking the said proceedings has expired and the respondent, without a judgment of this court extending the said delay, would be deprived of his right of defending himself and contesting the said petition above mentioned.
Whereas it is necessary that the respondent obtain the said continuation of delay to permit him to contest the said petition as he intends to do.



Whereas the respondent has strong grounds tor promoting this request in his own interest.
And whereas this court has the power to order the continuation of delay asked for by the respondent.
May it please the court to relieve the respondent from all default which could be brought against him under the law and which could be registered against him by the requirements of the order for delay granted by the law for contesting the petition as may be proper, and that the said request shall not commence to run or to count only from the date of the judgment of this honourable court on this present motion, and that it may be allowed to the respondent to contest the said petition, as he intends to do if granted the said delay.
Costs ought to follow the results.
Montreal, February 14, 1921.
Murphy, Gouin and Parent,
Solicitors for the respondent.
Here follows the affidavit:
I the undersigned Rodolphe Lemieux, barrister, of the City of Montreal, Province of Quebec, residing at 265 O'Connor street in the city of Ottawa, being duly sworn, depose and say:
1.	I am the respondent in the above mentioned cause.
2.	All the facts alleged in the above mentioned notice of motion are true to the best of my knowledge, and I have signed.
Rodolphe Lemieux. Sworn before Nathaniel Mills.
Notary Public.
That is the main part of the motion and is all I wish to quote.
There is only one word I have to say in connection with the debate which has been so prolonged. In answer to the hon. member for Maisonneuve, who says that the motion of the hon. member for Frontenac makes no charge. As I understand the motion it makes a deliberate charge of an attempt-a successful one, I think-to evade the rules of this House. That to my mind is a very serious charge if the hon. member for Maisonneuve is guilty of it. It seems to me that there is only one particular hand seen in this-the hand of the hon'. member for Maisonneuve. The hon. member for Lotbiniere to-day said that there was nothing to show that the hon. member for Maisonneuve engineered these delays. Why, he did it himself. He did not require to hire any one to pass on the action of the hon. member himself. The hon. member for Maisonneuve says that he really did not know the man, alleged to be his friend, who filed the petition. He has not told us that he ever tried to find out whether it was a friend or enemy. It is a queer thing that a man who had a petition brought against him and which had been pending for three years would not even today know the name of the pettioner, would not have intimated to the House that he

had made some inquiries to find out who the petitioner was, and on the whole it looks just a little suspicious that if the hon. gentleman did not engineer he at least propagated the attempt to delay the hearing of the petition from time to time by himself for-

If my hon. friend will
allow me? He says it is rather surprising that I should not know the petitioner, who is one of niy electors. I would put a question to my hon. friend: Does he know each one of his electors?

I would know the man
who made the charge. -

My hon. friend does
not represent a city constituency of that size. I declare that I do not know the petitioner, I have never seen him.

I accept the hon. gentleman's statement. I suppose his solicitors might easily have told him, if he had been very anxious to know, who was the gentleman who ostensibly took this serious proceeding against him. But I do not wish to labour the question. I rose mainly for the purpose of putting on record the affidavit which shows that the application for delay was put upon the court records by the hon. gentleman himself.

Will my hon. friend allow
me? Why does he not press the question in court as provided by law? He could appear in court or have some of his friends, for instance, any elector of Maisonneuve, appear in court and owing to the delay ask to be substituted for the petitioner in order to prosecute the petition.

The answer to that question would appeal to me like this, Mr. Speaker. If I were charged with corrupt practices and had a petition hanging over my head, I would be the first man to take advantage of the very rule the hon. gentleman speaks of, to have that petition dismissed on my own motion for want of prosecution. I suppose the hon. gentleman will not say that he could not have done that?
I do not follow the hon. gentleman. What does he say?
I asked the hon. gentleman if there was anything to prevent him from making a motion to dismiss that petition and have it taken off the files of the courts?

I do not know the
meaning of my hon. friend's question. But if he wants to know from me what intention I have-
No. If my hon. friend will allow me I will repeat my question.
My hon. friend is putting a question to me and trying to make it appear that I do not want to answer it.
No.
I would like to give a straight answer to my hon. friend.
I do not know how my hon. friend can give a straight answer when he does not understand my question.
My hon. friend is trying to impress the House with the idea that I am trying to evade his question.
I did not say that.

That I am trying to evade the process which would put an end to the petition one way or the other. I declare to the hon. gentleman that he is misinformed as to that, and that on the contrary I am anxious to get this petition dismissed. I intend on the morrow of this session to take proper proceedings to put an end to it. If my hon. friend will accept this assurance it may perhaps placate his conscience.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are getting into
very loose methods in this debate. The Chair has not seen fit to intervene and insist on the strict observance of the rules, because this being a question of privilege I thought the good sense of the House might be trusted not to depart too far from the rules. The debate has taken the whole afternoon, and I must now insist on a strict adherence to the rules. The hon. member would not be in order in submitting a question to the hon. member for Maison-neuve or any other hon. member.
I wished to answer my hon. friend.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman, Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must rule that the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy) is not in order in submitting a question to the hon. member for Maisonneuve.

Then I make the assertion that under the practices of all

I say-and I say it advisedly- that if the hon. gentleman was as anxious two years ago to get rid of this process as he professes to be now, he had under the law the right as respondent, in his own behalf to move for the dismissal of the petition from the files of the court.
