speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the remarks which I have to offer this evening on the motion submitted by the hon. member for Fron-tenac (Mr. Edwards) will be in one respect like the prayers recited at the funeral of Sir John Moore, "few and short". I felt, when listening to my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) this afternoon that he deserved the congratulations of all the members of the House for the moderation with which he introduced his motion. The hon. member has a reputation, at any rate in the province of Quebec, of being a somewhat fiery orator when he works himself up to the proper pitch. It is probable that he did not have the necessary confidence in his case this afternoon and it was that which caused him to speak in the tone he did. Per contra, I cannot offer my felicitations to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) for the manner in which they handled the question when it came before the House.
I propose to call for a vote when the House is ready for the same, on the principle whether we ought to permit a question of this kind to come before the Privileges and Elections Committee or any other committee of Parliament, rather than the courts under the Dominion Controverted Elections Act. There is more reason why this case should be disposed of under that Act than, perhaps, any case of this nature that has been before the House for a considerable time, and that is that it is now before the courts, and we propose by this motion to take the matter out of the hands of the judicial authorities and to cast it into the arena of Parliament. We ought not to take this attitude without careful consideration, because to do so will create a precedent which will work both ways. The principle of sending such

cases before the courts under the Dominion Controverted Elections Act has been enunciated in this House for nearly fifty years. In 1873 the Dominion Controverted Elections Act was passed, and since that time, with one or two exceptions, all matters of the kind now before the House, have been disposed of under that Act, and in this case we were following the precedents set up and established by the Imperial Parliament. The citation of the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien), this afternoon, is quite apposite and apropos. He was referring to a statement made by Sir John Thompson in 1887, when a matter of this kind was before the House, and I trust I may be permitted to read that citation once more, because I feel that the crux of the whole matter may be found in the remarks of Sir John Thompson. I am very sorry the Minister of Justice is not in his seat in order to hear the sapient words of his great predecessor in office, a constitutional lawyer of the very highest authority.
That extract, I think, was read this afternoon.

It cannot be read too often, because it evidently did not impress itself upon the Minister of Justice. Knowing the mentality of the Minister of Justice as I do-I was a student of his for three or four years-I think it will be advisable to cite it once more, because the matter is good and the Minister of Justice might benefit by giving it second thought. This is what Sir John Thompson says:
Since the change which I have referred to, and by which Parliament has renounced its rights to deal with the matter of controverted elections, there has been fully recognized in the various discussion's that have taken place In the Imperial House of Gammons, this principle-
Mark the words.
-that everything has been transferred to the judiciary in connection with controverted elections, excepting the one question of the disqualification of persons who have been returned to Parliament. As was said by Sir Henry James in 1882, in the case of Michael Havitt, the only question which Parliament has reserved to itself to deal with is the question whether a proper person has been returned in obedience to the writ.
That is the only question with which Parliament now deals.
As was explained by Lord Coleridge and Lord Selborne in a previous debate in 1870, that reservation is not in conflict with the statute which says that the election shall only be contested by an election petition, because the House has to consider whether the writ has been obeyed which commanded the electors of the shire, or the county, to return a suitable

person to sit in that House. The House, therefore, is still seized of the right to decide whether the writ has (been obeyed by the election of a person who is fit and proper to sit in that House.
He continues, and I would draw the attention of hon. gentlemen on the other side to these remarks:
But as soon as the question has been decided as to the qualification of the person so returned, the conduct of the returning officer, or the number of votes which were received, the conduct of the candidates, and every other question connected with the election, or with the conduct of the returning officer, has been relegated to the judiciary, and the House has always declined to exercise its functions and its power to interfere.
That is the practice in England, and it is a practice for which we contended in the Yukon election case which came before the House a couple of years ago. The hon. member for Quebec East in his address before the House on that occasion quoted from May's "Parliamentary Practice" the following:
Before the- year 1770, controverted elections were tried and determined by the whole House of Commons, as mere party questions, upon which the strength of contending factions might be tested.
So you will notice, Mr. Speaker, that the House, in order to obtain precedents for throwing this matter into the Privileges and Elections Committee, is obliged to grope back to the year 1770 and before that. He continues:
In order to prevent so notorious a perversion of justice-
Mark the words.
-the House consented to submit the exercise of its privilege to a tribunal constituted by law, which, though composed of its own members, should be appointed so as to secure impartiality, and the administration of justice according to the laws of the land, and under the sanction of oaths.
That is to say, they formed a Privileges and Elections Committee. Then he goes on:
This principle was maintained, with partial alterations of the means by which it was carried out, until 1868, when the jurisdiction of the House, in the trial of controverted elections was transferred by Statute to the courts of law.
In 1868, the rule was changed whereby all those matters were sent to the courts of law under the Controverted Elections Act. We followed, in 1873, with a somewhat similar statute, the Dominion Controverted Elections Act. Why cannot the courts deal with this question? Why is it necessary that it should be brought be-

fore Parliament? It was pointed out this afternoon by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. MeMaster) that section 30, subsection 2, gives any person, an elector in the division of Maisonneuve, the authority and power to proceed with a case where the petitioner refuses or fails to proceed. It is a simple matter for the Government to secure some person in the large electoral division of Maisonneuve to proceed with this petition. I fancy that it would be necessary to obtain some person whose views are favourable to the Government. Possibly the Government feels that it is impossible for it to obtain a single elector in the division of Maisonneuve who is sympathetic to the Government. That is the only reason why the Government is perhaps not proceeding. It is the simplest matter in the world for a petitioner, an ordinary person, an elector, to come before the court with a petition explaining' that he understands that there is collusion; that the case is not being proceeded with for the reasons mentioned in this House to-day, and he thereupon becomes a party to the suit. Why is it not proceeded with thus? In this way a decision would be obtained from a judicial tribunal. We all know what happens before the Privileges and Elections Committee. I am not a prophet, but I am perhaps bold enough to make the claim that I am descended from a race of prophets. I will tell the House what is going to happen. There will he two reports, one by the majority of the committee and the other by the minority. The majority will report along the lines hinted at by the Minister of Justice and by the Prime Minister. The minority will bring in a report-
The right report.

The right report, as my
hon. friend from Brome saysi, indicating that the conduct of all parties in connection with this matter is as white as the driven snow. Will that get us anywhere, Mr. Speaker? The public understand these things; the public is not a fool; the public knows, as every one in this House knows, that this incident is brought up merely for the purpose of making political capital out of it, and the report of the committee *will be affected very largely owing to the fact that it is brought in by a partisan majority.
I am sorry that the Prime Minister is not in his seat at the present moment, because I desire to put to him a question as to why Sir Rodolphe Forget was allowed
to sit on the Government benches for six years without any action at all being taken to make him elect for which of two seats he would sit. What is sauce for the goose is sauce for the gander, and in the case of Sir Rodolphe Forget, mind you, there were no contestation proceedings of any kind. Are hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House aware that during the parliamentary session hon. members need not proceed with their cases; they are not obliged to proceed with their cases while Parliament is in session. Are hon. gentlemen aware that since 1917 this House has been sitting in the aggregate for the best part of two years? In this connection I wish to cite section 39 of the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, which provides :
The trial of every election petition shall he commenced within six months from the time when suoh petition has been presented, and shall be proceeded with from day to day until such trial is over; but if, at any time, it appears to the court that the respondent's presence at the trial is necessary, such trial shall not be commenced during any session of Parliament, if the respondent is a member; and in the computation of any time or delay allowed for any step or proceeding in respect of any such trial, or for the commencement thereof as aforesaid, the time occupied by such session of Parliament shall not be included.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve was attending to his parliamentary duties here for nearly two years, when his case could not be proceeded with. Then we know, as he explained this afternoon, that he went to Europe after the session of 1919, and was away for nearly seven months, so that he has practically been away from the court where the case is to be tried for over two years. I submit that the Prime Minister, when he was discussing this question in all its phases this afternoon, and knowing of this provision in the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, must have overlooked the fact that the hon. member for Maisonneuve was not obliged to attend the term of the court during the entire time this House was in session.
I asked the right hon. the Prime Minister this afternoon if he was aware of the citation in Bourinot to the effect that this rule which it is complained is being broken has been more honoured in the breach than in the observance. Never before in the history of this Parliament, I venture to say, never since Confederation, at any rate, has a question of this kind come before the House. Why, then, is this matter trotted out to-day before the House, and political capital attempted to be made out of it? The answer, Mr. Speaker, is

so obvious that it does not need to be given. We have been told here to-day of several recent cases of hon. gentlemen with a seat in this House with a dual mandate. The ex-Prime Minister of this country, the right hon. gentleman who has just recently retired a few years ago, if I remember well, occupied two seats. - Sir Wilfrid Laurier also occupied two seats, and there are other like cases.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve this afternoon stated that he was perfectly willing to go before the Privileges and Elections Committee, as he had nothing to disguise, and was afraid of nothing that might come up. He felt that his skirts were clear, and he wanted the matter brought before any tribunal whatever as soon as it possibly could be brought. He may be right in that. I suppose he is justified in asking that the Privileges and Elections Committee handle this case forthwith, but personally I shall object to this motion being passed without a vote being-taken even if I should be the only one to vote for allowing this matter to remain with the courts and for depriving the Privileges and Elections Committee of the opportunity of dealing with it. It is because of the principle for which we have been struggling in this country and in this House for many years. It is a principle that was laid down long before many of us were born. It is not a question of whose case is coming-before the House at the present moment. It is a question of principle. Are we prepared to go back to the year 1770, or are we prepared to maintain the principle that in every case arising out of elections, except that of the disqualification of the person returned, the matter must go before the courts?
The hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) deplored to-day that we have no federal courts to' deal with this matter. He thought it was somewhat of an anomaly that a federal matter of this sort should not be dealt with by a federal court. I would point qut to the hon. gentleman and to the House that the court before which this case is to be tried is a federal court. It is a court which interprets the Dominion Controverted Elections Act, a federal statute. The judge who sits on that court is a federal judge; he draws his salary from the Dominion treasury, and he sits as a federal judge.
Under all these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I cannot see why there is such an insistent demand on the part of the leaders on the Government side that this matter shall be taken before the Privileges
IMr. Jacobs.]
and Elections Committee. As I said before, it will get us nowhere. It will provoke a considerable amount of srife. This case should be settled by the court which is seized of it, and I venture to say that if our friends on the Government side are as anxious as they claim to be to have this seat vacated, if they would see that the machinery provided by the law under the Dominion Controverted Elections, Act was put in motion, they would very soon get what they desire.

Mr. Speaker, there may be some excuse for hon. members supporting the Government or the Opposition voting on questions for purely party reasons, but there can be no such excuse for the members of the Progressive party. The country will listen to no such excuse from us. We must vote according to our convictions, or we will be condemned.
Convicted.

Some may think that
is rather an unfortunate position to be in, but I am rather inclined to think it is the reverse. The hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) has indicated a way in which any person who wishes this matter settled can have it disposed of, but some question has been raised as to the procedure he suggested. There seems to have been no objection raised, however, to the procedure suggested by my hon. friend from Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe). We must assume therefore that there is no legal objection which can be advanced to the plan suggested by him. It is quite apparent that the speakers on the Government side admit the correctness of his position, because they are offering no objection to it. It has been suggested by the Prime Minister and others that a definite charge or allegation has been made. Well, I listened carefully to my hon. friend from Erontenac (Mr. Edwards), who usually is very easily understood, and I failed to hear from him anything in the nature of a definite accusation or charge at all. It is true he made some suggestion that the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux), was evading the rules of the House, but that is very sweeping; it is like calling a man a thief without formulating any definite charge of theft against him. That, of course, is a common thing in this world, and we do not usually take such insinuations seriously. Not only has there been no definite charge, but the hon. member for Maisonneuve has distinctly

denied that there was any evasion or collusion on his part. That statement was quite decided; it was the most distinct statement we have heard in this debate.
The member for Frontenac, in support of his insinuation that there is something wrong, that there is some collusion, advances several arguments, the principal one upon which he chiefly depends being, apparently, the fact that the hon. member for Maisonneuve, the respondent in the case, has not compelled the prosecutor-in this matter, the petitioner-to proceed, or in default, asked that the case be dismissed. I suppose my hon. friend, although not a lawyer, is perfectly aware that this is the privilege of every defendant; and I wonder, if the member for Frontenac were a lawyer, how often he would advise the adoption of the procedure which he now suggests. The first case I ever had in my life was one in which I followed that procedure, and although it came out all right in the end I never followed it again. I have always followed the policy which every sane lawyer usually follows, that of letting sleeping dogs lie. How many lawyers in this House are in the habit of taking advantage of the right of forcing the prosecution to proceed? I am afraid that such lawyers would not have many clients or for long. This is true in ordinary cases, and it is doubly true in cases of election protests. I wonder if there is a single lawyer in this House who has ever done as my hon. friend suggests. Surely there is not a lawyer living who has ever followed the policy which the hon. member for Frontenac seems to think should be followed. If any lawyer did so, then I think he should immediately be examined by an alienist to decide whether he should practice at the bar, or be removed to a lunatic asylum; the chances would be overwhelmingly in favour of his confinement in an asylum rather than allowing him to continue practising. Any one can understand the reasonableness of this. How many elections are fought in this country when? a man elected, be he ever so honest and honourable, is positively certain that no improper proceeedings have been taken by any one to elect him? I think that most hon. gentlemen in this House won their election, so far as they are personally concerned, quite honestly. I have no doubt at all about that, and I cast no reflections on anyone.
Which side of the House?

On either side. But how many hon. members are absolutely sure that not a single person connected with their election used improper means during the campaign? In view of the uncertainty of that situation, would not a lawyer he a positive fool to advise such procedure as the member for Frontenac proposes and which he seems to think there is some crookedness in not carrying out? The mere statement of the case shows the absurdity of the hon. member's position. Now, there is an old legal maxim which says that he who comes to equity must come with clean hands. Are hon. members who have addressed us from the other side this afternoon coming with clean hands? Did not all those hon. gentlemen in the last Parliament sit along with a man who was guilty of exactly what they suggest that possibly my hon. friend from Maisonneuve may be guilty of? There seems to be no question as to the other gentleman having violated the rule, but I never heard that any objection was taken by hon. gentlemen opposite to his sitting in the House.
Who was that?

Sir Rodolphe Forget, with whom my hon. friend from Frontenac probably sat in this House. Surqly no man can suggest for a moment that men who sat with that gentleman for a whole term, without raising any objection, have the right now to raise such a tremendous row because, in their opinion, there is a possibility that the hon. member for Maisonneuve may be guilty of the same offence which they overlooked in one of their own.
They are becoming virtuous before death.

Then we shall have to send for the higfh priest. Surely hon. gentlemen opposite cannot pretend that they are coming into court with clean hands. When they winked at what they tacitly admit was a wrong on their own side, they cannot reasonably suggest that there should be a thorough examination of something on the part of the hon. member for Maisonneuve in connection with which there is no definite charge. Now, insinuations were thrown across the House this afternoon, and they have been at other times for that matter, against the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). With those insinuations I do not identify myself, but it has been suggested that the right hon. gentleman has been evading the spirit of the law in

drawing superannuation as well as his pay as a minister and his indemnity as a member of Parliament. I am not saying that he has evaded the law, but that insinuation has been thrown out. Are our hon. friends on the other side suggesting that an investigation into that alleged evasion of the law be instituted and carried out? They are not. Why? Because he sits on that side.
Do you say it is an evasion of any law?

I do not say so, but the suggestion has been made on this side of the House by different members, and it is merely in keeping with the insinuation of my hon. friend opposite (Mr. Edwards), that there is something in connection with the member for Maisonneuve that should be investigated. Personally, I am not saying that the Minister of Justice is guilty of an evasion of the law.
It is an invasion of the law.

I do say, however,
that if the right hon. gentleman were on the Opposition side there would be suggestions for an investigation, especially if he were in this unfortunate group of Progressives. Now, let hon. members be fair; let them play the game fairly like men and not try to play politics, because this is nothing but party politics. The hon. member for Maisonneuve has stated that he will welcome an investigation. I do not know what action will be taken on the strength of that declaration, but I will say that while I have no serious objection to this matter going to the committee, with the consent of the hon. member for Maisonneuve, if there is to be a vote on the question I cannot see how any man who acts conscientiously according to his convictions, as we should act, can refuse to vote against the proposal.

Mr. Speaker, if it is a matter of conscience on the part of my hon. friend from Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) to have to take the position that he has taken, I suppose it is the privilege of every other hon. member of the House to pursue the course which he is going to follow for the same reason. The question before the House is a very simple one. The hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) claims that the privileges of the House have been violated by the fact that an hon. member 
is occupying two seats at the same time. The hon. gentleman in question, who represents the counties of Gaspe and Maisonneuve, claims that he has not violated the privileges of the House. That is all there is to be decided. The hon. member for Frontenac, believing that the privileges of the House have been violated, has asked that this question be referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections. The hon. member for Gaspe and Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), speaking from his place welcomes a reference to that committee. Why? Because in view of the circumstances which surround his position it is an act of justice and of fair play to him to decide whether the charge is well founded. Why should we refuse to accord justice and fair play to one of our colleagues when the issue, according to his own declaration, has been put before the House in a calm and dignified manner and with every apparent desire to reach a just decision?

What would happen if
the Committee on Privileges and Elections were to decide that the hon. gentleman has violated the privileges of the House and the court were to decide that he has not?

If my hon. friend
wants to know in advance what will be the result of the inquiry before the committee and what judgment the court will render, to my mind ihe is not discussing the question at present before the House. The question is this: an hon. member of this House is charged with having violated one of its privileges, and the only way to do him justice is to support the stand that he has taken himself. The hon. gentleman says, "I have never violated any of the privileges of the House. I am willing to go before the committee and explain the stand that I have taken." The hon. gentleman expects that justice will be done him; why then should we refuse to give him the benefit of the position that he has taken? In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would remind those horn gentlemen who, with the best of intentions I am sure, have undertaken the defence of the hon. member who represents the counties of Gasp6 and Maisonneuve-
I require no defence.
I undertook none.

If the hon. members who have seen fit to defend the stand taken by the hon. gentleman who represents in this chamber the two counties of Gaspe and Maisonneuve keep on refusing to agree

to this matter being referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections surely, quoting the words of Frederick the Great,
I would say if I were in the position of the hon. gentleman, "The Lord deliver me from my friends. Give me my foes and I will take care of them."

I suppose the first
words I should utter should be words of appreciation to the hon. member for Gaspe and Maisonneuve for having been good enough to say that I have surprised him by being less partisan and more judicial than he expected. I accept with gratitude this double-headed compliment coming from my hon. friend. I should not pass without notice the appreciative utterance of my genial friend who represents the' constituency of George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) along the same line. That hon. gentleman interpolated the remark when the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Thomson) was speaking that we were becoming virtuous before death.
Hear, hear.

It occurs to us, Mr. Speaker, that even that belated virtue is preferable to none at all. The only inference I could draw from the remark is, that while the hon. gentleman credited us with a desire to be virtuous at some time during our lives he did not hint that such a thing is possible to the members on his own side. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark) intimated that in some way I was lacking in appreciation of what was due the House and the country in my attitude with respect to the matter of the by-elections. Well, I was flattering myself that in that matter I had taken the same position as the hon. member himself and what greater honour could a man have, either here or in the country, than to find himself ranged on the same side as the hon. member for Red Deer on any question?1 Yet my hon. friend is not disposed to give me even that morsel of comfort. He spoke on that matter rather caustically, so far as I was concerned, and plumed himself on taking a virtuous and very proper stand, but he is not willing that I should get any credit although I took the same stand as he did.
Keep it up, though.

No, Mr. Speaker, I can assure my hon. friend from Red Deer that my muscles, and body are such that I cannot attempt-to follow my hon. friend
in his political * career. I do not see how any person could successfully do so unless he had the physical qualities of a snake. My hon. friend from Qu'Appelle, speaking as a lawyer, says, "It is ridiculous to suppose that the respondent, or the defendant, in the case would try and press this matter to a conclusion," and he puts this question to me: How often would the member for Frontenac, if he were a lawyer, follow the course which he has intimated should have been followed by the hon. member for Maisonneuve and Gaspe, the respondent in this case? I think I can answer that question, though I am not a lawyer. If I were a lawyer, and a man came to me with a case such as this in which he was the respondent, I would advise him, if I thought he had a weak case, to follow the course of delay. That is just exactly what I think the hon. member for Qu'Appelle said he would advise, and that is what any lawyer would advise unless he was a fool. But if I felt my client had a good case and I could dispose of it successfully for him, then I would advise him to go ahead. I would say to him: "If the petitioner will not press it, you ask to have the case dismissed. That will show your bona tides, and people will know that they must not bring such actions against you in future unless they have a good foundation for them."
Now, Sir, the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) confirmed me in the position which I took in asking for support of this resolution, and several of the statements made by that hon. gentleman were repeated by others. He said that any elector could ask for the petition to be proceeded with or to have it dismissed. Well, I think that view was concurred in by several other hon. members, and also by the hon. member for Gaspe and Maisonneuve himself. If any elector could have asked that this case be dismissed because the petitioner had not proceeded as he should have done, then why did not the member who was most interested take that course? Why do hon. gentlemen opposite throw the onus on this side of the House for not instituting proceedings along that line? The man most interested was the respondent. Was there anything to prevent him taking action? He did not take action.
Let me call attention for a moment to one or two other matters. The hon. member for Gaspe and Maisonneuve gave certain reasons why no move was made on his

part to have the petition dismissed because of lack of action on the part of the petitioner. He said that for part of the year he was busy here as a member of Parliament, and that after the session was over there were legal holidays, and that in 1919 he spent a considerable time in Europe. Now, I would immediately absolve my hon. friend in regard to the year 1919. I think I know why he went overseas, and so far as that period is concerned let us leave it out of the question altogether. But in all fairness-and I want to be fair in discussing this matter-let us look at the other years. He had the year 1918, and the year 1920, but he took no action in either of those years. Now, it has been stated that when the House was in session certain restrictions operated against this case being proceeded with. I think I am right in saying that during the session the petitioner could not proceed with the petition, nor could any hon. member. But there was one person to whom that restriction did not apply, and that was the respondent in the case. While I or any person else would be debarred from applying to the court to have the case gone on with or dismissed while the House was in session, because such action would constitute interference with the rights of the hon. member, he himself could have proceeded to have the petition dealt with. But my hon. friend says that his time was pretty well taken up; he is a very busy man. Well, I am willing to accept that statement. However, although he is a very busy man, he is very much concerned in having this matter dealt with. But while he pleads those excuses for not taking steps to have the petition dismissed, he did find time to ask of his own motion on two occasions this year for delay, first, when he engaged other legal advisers, and subsequently, on"*February 21. That action on my hon. friend's part took place just a few days after this session was called, and while by taking those steps he did not prevent himself from proceeding further, he did prevent any person else,from taking up the case. I think my argument is sound and that the hon. gentleman cannot and will not attempt to dispute it.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have given reasons why in my estimation this whole matter should be referred to the committee on Privileges and Elections. Hon. gentlemen have adverted to the fact that Sir Ro-dolphe Forget sat for two seats between 1908 and 1911, I think.
Between 1911 and 1917.

And I think I am right in saying that the late right hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier sat for two seats in the same Parliament. No action was taken by members on either side of the House. Well, I do not think that is a very good reason why action should not be taken in this case. Once more let me say this: for many years it was recognized that hon. gentlemen might run for two constituencies. No outcry was made against that practice; it was followed by members on both sides. But in the fall session of 1919 this Parliament took a very definite stand in regard to the filling of vacancies. Prior to that time it had been the custom for the Government to exercise its right to call a by-election whenever it saw fit, and sometimes the by-elections would be held soon after a vacancy, sometimes after considerable delay. That practice, I say, had been followed by both parties from time immemorial. But after a careful study of the question hon. members of this House came to the unanimous conclusion that that was not a right system to follow and an Act was unanimously passed restricting to six months the time within which any vacancy must be filled by by-election. By taking that step we declared that the customs and practices which had prevailed for thirty, forty or fifty years should not continue; therefore it is illogical that we should allow any constituency to remain vacant for a matter of five sessions.
I do not think that the law of 1919 was retroactive in its effect.

It is not a question of merely thinking so; my hon. friend knows that it was not retroactive in its effect. But that had nothing to do with the matter. In 1919 we passed an Act by which it was stated to be wrong for any constituency to be unrepresented in this House for longer than six months, and in which the Government was called upon to take action to see that that sort of think did not occur. In the debate which took place on that occasion the matter of my hon. friend's holding these two seats was brought to his attention by my hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy). Even, therefore, if my hon. friend had not prior to that time taken any action to have this ease dealt with, he was given notice at least by one hon. member as to how some felt in regard to his holding two seats. I submit that he has had ample opportunity since the fall session of 1919-to go no further back than

that-to have the question definitely settled and one of these constituencies directly represented in this House.
The position that we are in to-day is entirely different from that which the parties were in prior to the passing of the Act respecting by-elections in the fall session of 1919. At that time we took a definite stand in regard to a definite matter and I contend that that does have a bearing upon the vacancy, if I may call it so, which exists in one of these constituencies at the present time-not a vacancy in the technical sense of the term, but a vacancy nevertheless.
I pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend did have an opportunity to bring this case to a settlement. I referred him this afternoon to section 19A of the Dominion Controverted Elections Act which provided that after the expiration of fifteen days upon the application
9 p.m. of either party, the time and place for trial should be fixed.
I pointed out that my hon. friend, for the purposes of this case, is one of the "either parties" referred to, and that he had an opportunity under that section to take action. He has not denied that; he has admitted that he could, had he so chosen, have had this matter brought to trial or have made a move to bring about the dismissal of the petition. He has admitted that; he cannot do otherwise in the face of the facts which have been laid before him. Is he to escape criticism because of his lack of action in that regard, especially in view of his assertion in this House that he regarded the holding of two seats by any member as undemocratic, as something which should not prevail in this country? But the hon. gentleman took no action whatever to put an end to that state of things so far as he was concerned. Again, under section 39 he had an opportunity to bring his case to trial and have it settled, but he took no action under that section either. He cannot, therefore, escape criticism for his lack of action in having this matter disposed of. It is all right enough for my hon. friends to say that it was a simple matter to have it disposed of by the courts; that any person could have asked the court to take action, and so on. If that is so why did not he-the man most interested, the man who felt that the principle of democracy was being violated-why did not he himself take action in regard to the matter?
My hon. friend has said that these long delays do look strange. He admitted that this afternoon; he said:	"I know it looks
strange." Yes, it. does; and who is responsible for its looking strange?
Without the explanation I gave.

eeedings, that is evideriee to me that this is not in the ordinary category of cases of this kind; that this is somewhat peculiar in many of its features, or, as the hon. gentleman himself says, that it looks very strange. Not only does it look strange to me; but the attitude of hon. gentlemen opposite looks very strange to me when I remember the attitude of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he arose and worked himself into a state of indignation over the fact that certain constituencies were not represented in this House; that certain by-elections had not been held, thus keeping certain constituencies vacant for a matter of one or two, or possibly three months. What an outrage it was upon the public of the Dominion of Canada that the Government did not bring those by-elections on at once! We all remember how the hon. gentleman went on in this House in regard to that matter. How does my hon. friend's attitude in regard to that look if it is placed alongside his complacent attitude in regard to the hon. gentleman sitting on his immediate right who has deprived one constituency in this country of representation in this House for five sessions? These are things which look strange-I use the word of my hon. friend himself. Having regard to the fact that my hon. friend had it within his power under the statute to move to have this petition dismissed because of non-action on the part of the petitioner, and that he took no action but, on the contrary, made motions to extend the delay, I say that these are things which look suspicious, which cast a shadow of doubt over the bona fide of the whole matter, at least in my mind, and, I believe, in the minds of many.
The hon. gentleman was good enough to say-and he was commended for his words by the former Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden)-that personally he was willing to come before the Privileges and Elections Committee and have the whole matter investigated. That is what I would expect of him, what I would expect of any hon. gentleman in a case of this kind. If he is confident, as his words would lead us to believe, of his position as regards any protest what has he to lose in having this matter brought before the Priviliges and Elections Committee? What has he to gain? No person has questioned my statement that the attitude of the petitioner in this case is most peculiar and has been so from the start. Then I say that the hon. gentleman has something to gain in this House in having this matter investigated by the Privileges and Elections Com-

mittee, by showing the attitude of the petitioner, by exposing his hand, by seeing why he has taken this very peculiar, strange attitude, why he has entered a petition which he apparently has no intention of following up. He must have known, as we all know, that as long as that petition pends, the hon. gentleman occupies two seats in this House.
I take the stand here, as I have taken it before, as I have a right to take it whether I am right in my conception of what will occur or not, that, having regard to the votes polled in those constituencies in 1911 when the issue was what must be the issue to a very large extent in the next election, I believe these hon. gentlemen are afraid to open either of those constituencies and test the public opinion. That is my view, and I cannot help thinking that this whole thing has been worked for the purpose of preventing an election in either of those constituencies. I have been long enough in politics to understand what this would mean. If an election were held in the constituency of Gaspe which gave a majority of 570 against my hon. friend in the election of 1911, a constituency which had been held by his party for years and years, and the election happened to go against this hon. gentleman, some of that prestige in the province of Quebec which the leader of the Opposition prides himself on having, would disappear. My hon. friend is an astute politician, and he does not want to take any chance in the matter. That is how it appears to me, and that is, perhaps, one reason why this petition has not been gone on with and the "petitioner has disregarded it entirely, and the hon member most affected has not availed himself of the opportunity to bring the matter to a conclusion.

If my hon. friend's
motion carries and the committee should make a report, showing that his suspicions were well founded; that there was no bona-fide petition and so on, does he think that would have the effect of dismissing the petition before the court of Montreal, or does he think that the petition would not have to be disposed of before my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) elects for one seat? If the latter be the case, what is the practical effect of my hon friend's motion?

Certainly, it would not dispose of the matter before the court. The hon. member for Gaspe and Maison-neuve stated in this House this afternoon just before six o'clock, his intention, on the day following the close of this session, to

take steps to bring this matter to a head. If he is willing to do that at the close of this session, why did he not take action along that line at the end of some other session? He could have taken action four times. He has declared that he will take action as soon as this session is over. I do not know whether he is going to do that regardless of legal holiadys or not We have had this matter dragging along and no action being taken in the courts, and we have surrounding it certain very suspicious actions on the part of the petitioner and, I must say, actions on the part of the respondent, that do not satisfy me that he has done all that he could do. At all events, if the Privileges and Elections Committee have an opportunity to go into the facts of this matter we shall have all the facts. My hon. friend says that he has nothing to, fear in a disclosure of the facts. Then he should not oppose this matter going to the committee, and if he is satisfied-and I think he intimated that he was satisfied to have it go there-why should these hon. gentlemen who are taking up the case on his side oppose my motion? For these reasons, I ask that the House register its opinion in favour of my motion.

speechtext: House again in committee on Bill No. 23 (from the Senate), respecting the Lake of the Woods Control Board, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When this Bill was last before the committee, clause 1 had been adopted.
On section 2-creation of board:

This Bill affects my
riding, and I therefore desire to say a few words upon it. It is creating quite a bit of dissension in certain parts of the district because the subject is not fully understood and the parties are not in complete accord. There are two towns side by side, Kenora and Keewatin. Kenora has been opposing the Bill, while Keewatin supports it. In my opinion there is no doubt as to be advisability of having control by both Governments, the Ontario and the Federal; but I doubt very much, in view of the manner in which the Bill was initiated, whether we shall secure concurrence in it from the

Ontario Legislature if we press the matter now. Three things are asked for; first, the control of the Norman dam, second, the control of the English river, and, third, the control in the province of Ontario of the Winnipeg river. As the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Meighen) pointed out when introducing the Bill, there should be no difficulty about the control of the Norman dam, which is a dam that really comes within the purview of the Dominion Government, became it affects navigation. It has never received the Dominion Government's assent, and, if necessary, that Government can at any time step in and take control of it. Control is provided for today under Orders in Council, and the purpose'of this Bill is to make that control by Act of Parliament; and it goes further and assumes control of the English river and of the powers on the Winnipeg river. That is purely a question for the Ontario Government, and if we pass this Bill and the Ontario Government does not pass a similar measure, then the Bill for that reason will be futile. Upon the Winnipeg river-there is a rapid or fall known as the White Dog Rapids for which a lease is about to be issued by the Ontario Government to a Mr. Backus and his associates for a power plant, and that intended lease is responsible for the initiation of this Bill. It is advisable to have control generally. There is control to-day as regards the Norman dam, which affects also international waters, and the matter could be temporarily arranged until all parties can see alike and agree upon all other points. I would suggest that as the Bill is of no virtue whatever unless passed by the Ontario Legislature, where so far it has been held up, it would be wise for us to wait and see what they will do. There is such a thing as being fortiter in re and there is also the suaviter in modo, and people do not like to have anything rammed down their troats. My constituents in Kenora are protesting against the Bill because they do not understand the position, and it would be well if the parties could get together and talk the matter over and see if they could not agree. The Kenora people need control there just as much as anyone else; and Keewatin wants control and should' have it. In regard to the level of the lake, the matter has been the subject of an international reference. It is not the fault of the Government that there is misunderstanding by the Kenora people; it is the fault of the Government officials, who consulted 149
only one side, the interests about which they were concerned, as the landlords, if one may use that term, of the Winnipeg power. They should, and could easily, have consulted the people of Kenora who are also vitally interested. They did not do so until after the Bill had been introduced, then they were called down and they felt angry and disappointed. It is of great importance to Canada, on account of her water powers in Manitoba, and of importance to Ontario and the power interests there, as well as of importance to the English river, to have the water all regulated in the wisest manner; but this can be done only by agreement. You cannot force it upon the people, and in my judgment it would be wiser to allow the Bill to stand with a view to securing that agreement. No harm could be done if the matter had even to be left in abeyance until next session, if _ a unanimous agreement were meanwhile reached.

Has a similar Bill
been introduced in Ontario?

I understand that a
similar Bill was introduced in the Ontario Legislature and given a first reading, but it has been held up. There is another point I want to mention about the Bill. It is only fair that if there be any interference in any way with any person's rights, the Bill should provide for some compensation; otherwise it would simply be confiscation without compensation. The Norman dam is, under this Bill, to be taken charge of by the joint board. The Kenora dam was built by a private concern, the Keewatin Power Company, and has since been sold. It is highly essential that the waters of the lake should be regulated for the benefit of all other interests on the lake. It is not now a satisfactory power site and may never be used as such; but it is unfair, if the dam is to be taken control of and regulated against the will of the owners, that they should not receive some kind of compensation. I have forgotten the details of the matter, but there was some arrangement on the part of one of the governments, either the Ontario Government or the Dominion, by which the sum of $4,000 was paid to secure the right of government control. If that dam were not there one would have to he built; but as it is there and is to be taken over for regulation purposes, I think that if there is any interference with any person's rights, there should be compensation for any damage

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
While the hon. member (Mr. Keefer), and I see eye to eye on the merits of the Bill-I am not able to discern any difference of opinion on that question-we have not, I must confess, been able to see eye to eye as to the wisdom of the moment for asking for its second reading and adoption by the House. The hon. member, of course, represents his constituency, and I am aware that what he says is correct, that there is a difference of opinion, as to the desirability of this legislation, between the different parts of his constituency. As regards his contention that something might be gained by delay in the way of getting the parties together, all I have to say is that we have already met the various parties to the controversy and have heard, with all eagerness and sincerity, their views upon the matter, and after so hearing them we feel that we can put forward no justification for withdrawing or delaying the legislation now before the House. In answer to the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) some days ago I think I stated, in my review of the case, that a conference had been held between the representatives of the province of Ontario including the Prime Minister, representatives of Manitoba including the Attorney-General, and representatives of the Dominion Government including myself and the Minister of the Interior, accompanied in the several cases by the proper officers concerned, and after the most thorough review this legislation was agreed upon to be introduced concurrently and passed concurrently, if acceptable to the respective legislatures, by Ontario on the one hand and by the Dominion on the other. The legislation has accordingly been introduced in the Ontario Legislature and that some time ago. Its passage has been delayed, however, the Prime Minister of Ontario desiring to give further opportunity for parties disagreeing therewith to be heard. He has, so far as I know, heard all parties and I am not aware that he is now delaying the measure at all. If he is I am not conversant with the reason.

In so far as Canada is concerned, pursuant to the agreement, we introduced a measure a month or more ago, passed it through the Senate and introduced it in this House, and have since not been able to proceed because of the desirability of getting on with Supply. There is nb saying how long the Ontario Legislature will be sitting; it will likely prorogue before long. I do think-and this is my opinion which I submit to the Committee-that it is our duty to consider the measure and deal with it now and not be in the position of having deferred it until the province of Ontario acted, or declined to act, and prorogued. In so far as the Government is concerned we agreed on the legislation. We believe the legislation is necessary, and we think it is in the public interest

we have not the least doubt about it. I gathered from the remarks of the hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) that in that respect he is at one with us. Consequently I cannot see how we can justify hanging back and saying "It is for you, the Government of Ontario, to pass this and if you do we will go ahead." I think our responsibility is at least equal to theirs; indeed, if there is any difference, I think it is the greater. This legislation on the part of both Houses is, in my judgment, essential, and I do not feel like being a party to a proceeding which seeks to evade any responsibility whatever. I think we ought to go ahead, and, so far as we are concerned, discharge our responsibility. As for the province of Ontario that is not for us to consider; that is their affair. There is no desire in the world to hasten the matter, but inasmuch as the session of the Ontario Legislature is of short duration it would in my judgment be undesirable for this House to let the Bill stand and, as it were, seek to shoulder the primary responsibility on Ontario. In my judgment there is no primary responsibility on them at all-it is just as much on us as on them.
The question then is whether the legislation is necessary. As to that I do not think there should be the least doubt. The control of the Lake of the Woods water system is vital. It is vital that this Government and this country assert and exercise that control to the extent of their interest. It is vital that Ontario assert and exercise it in so far as their interests are concerned. What are our interests and what are theirs? Our interests arise first because it is an international body of water. Shall it be argued for-a minute that it should be left to private interests,-the owners of

the Norman dam for instance at the outlet of the Lake of the Woods,-to have control of the levels that they virtually have to-day and that, they exercising the control, we should be liable for the failure to exercise control in the public interest? We should be liable if, for example, they should so control the level of the Lake of the Woods as to produce flood waters in Minnesota; it is this Parliament and this country that is going to be responsible then. Why therefore should the control of the level of the Lake of the Woods be left to the caprice of private parties? From that source therefore one source of our responsibility arises.
Another is this: our responsibility is not only centrally and exclusively our own but it is paramount in relation to navigation, and the question of maintaining the levels properly for the purposes of navigation is our responsibility and our responsibility alone. Hitherto it has been exercised by some joint arrangement between the province of Ontario and the Keewatin Power Company, now the property of Mr. Backus, the owners of the Norman dam. It surely is not becoming that this Parliament, having imposed upon it by the constitution a distinct jurisdiction and duty should leave to the province of Ontario and Mr. Backus, or the Keewatin Power Company, the carrying out of that duty? That is ours and we cannot fail to exercise it.
I have stated to the committee what is the interest of Canada federally in this matter. The interest of Ontario arises because they are the owners of the power properties of the water in that province We are the owners and administrators of the power properties farther down in Manitoba; that is still a third derivation of our duties in the matter. But Ontario is the owner so far as its interests are concerned; consequently it is not right that the exercise of this control should be carried on without reference to that province. That is where the joint legislation is necessary. It may be asked: " Why is it we are coming in now, and now only, to exercise it?" The reason is that for many years the control of the Norman dam, and through it of the level of the Lake of the Woods, was exercised by some sort of agreement between the Keewatin Power Company an ;1 the province of Ontario. During the continuance of this agreement-and remember neither party to that agreement had any constitutional jurisdiction at all to regulate the levels of the Lake of the Woods- but during this agreement the International Joint Commission sat and deliberated upon
149J
the question as to how the whole problem -power, navigation, navigable streams, all phases of it-should be taken care of. They have made a report. Canada accedes to that report. The United States, as yet, has not wholly acceded to it. They take some minor objections but substantially they are in accord with Canada. Now all this Bill seeks to do is to take care of the situation in the meantime in accordance with the finding of the report, to take care of the levels of the Lake of the Woods for the purposes of navigation and power in a manner wholly consonant with the verdict of the International Joint Commission, and in this respect not in any way dissented from by the United States of America. But up to now for the space of about two years this has been done by the Lake of the Woods Control Board, half of whom were nominated by Ontario and half by the Dominion. But that board derived its jurisdiction wholly by Order in Council, and it is doubtful whether that jurisdiction is legally well founded or not. At all events the board has appealed to place its jurisdiction on a more secure foundation, and the purpose of this Bill is to place -that authority on that secure and indisputable foundation, and further to more specifically declare just what its authority is.
Now I have sought to uphold the principle of the measure and its terms generally, although I know those are not disputed by the hon. member for Rainy River. I have laid before the committee, though, as well, my reasons for believing that this House would not be justified in merely standing aside and waiting for action on the part of the province of Ontario. In my judgment-and I speak in this respect for the Government generally -it is of first importance that having come to this arrangement in the public interest, we should go right ahead and carry it out and seek to establish the board upon the secure foundation which it will be established upon if this legislation is passed, and then leave it to the province of Ontario to go on with their side of the arrangement or not, as they may see fit.
I hope I am not wrong when I express the belief that they will not fail to go ahead and carry out the arrangement as originally devised and agreed upon; I do not think they will. I earnestly trust that they will continue to agree with the view of this Government, that the control of the level and of the outlet of the Lake of the Woods and of all the powers as well as the navigation interests depending there-

on must be a matter of governmental jurisdiction in the interests of all the people of the Dominion generally, and of Manitoba and Ontario particularly, and that no private interest must be permitted to assert that it is in a position to exercise any control, derivable from purchase or otherwise, because such control necessarily must be a prerogative of government, and of government alone.

In order to make it
perfectly clear, no one contends or has contended that control of the Lake of the Woods should or would be in private hands. That would be a most serious mistake. There is not that private control there now. The Dominion Government has always power to step in and exercise control, but subject to compensation, I suppose. We do need the co-operation of the province of Ontario so far as the English river is concerned, which is a branch of the Winnipeg river that does not flow into the Lake of the Woods and is below the Norman dam. We cannot step in there alone and take control. We do need also their co-operation on the Winnipeg river below the Norman dam, and for that reason we should endeavour to get this arrangement worked out amicably. But I would like again to make it perfectly clear that no person I know of has ever advocated that the control of the Lake of the Woods should be in the hands of private persons. The town of Kenora, which is directly interested in this matter, does not advocate private control. There should be Government control, even federal control alone if necessary; but there should also be federal and provincial control of the other two branches, the English river and the Winnipeg river.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 3-purposes:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Meighen moves
to amend clause 3 by inserting after the word "secure" in the first line thereof the words "severally and", and by adding at the end of the clause the words, "save and excepting the operation and control of all dams and regulating works extending across the international boundary, and the dam and regulating works across the Canadian channel at Kettle Falls."

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Amendment agreed to.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 5-general powers-enfoi cement of orders by rules of court:
£Mr. Meighen.]

I notice we are giving power to this commission to carry out the effect of any Act that may be passed by the province of Ontario. I can understand that the Legislature of Ontario would have power to say that the Act will be carried out by this board, but I do not quite understand how we can say that our board can carry out the provisions of any Act passed by the legislature.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. member is probably right, and that so far as this Parliament is concerned the clause has no effect at all. But it has effect so far as Ontario is concerned, arising from the fact that the legislation is concurrent.
Do I understand that identical legislation has been introduced in the Ontario Legislature?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes, it has been introduced there.
And also in the Manitoba Legislature?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, they do not need it, because this Parliament has control of the water powers in Manitoba.

I understand that this is an arrangement between the Dominion and the Provincial Governments and is the only feasible way of carrying out what is desirable. But I hope the Government have clearly before them the fact that the Winnipeg river is navigable, and as such the water powers there belong to the Dominion Government. This clause 5, leaving to the Legislature of the province of Ontario full power, ought to be guarded, for the reason that the province no doubt contends that the water powers on these small rivers belong to them. I think the Dominion has given way or silently acquiesced in the appropriation of many water powers which belong to the Dominion. The Niagara river is navigable, although it is not navigable at the great declivity at the Falls, and yet the Dominion is getting no value out of the water powers which really belong to it. This raises a great constitutional question, and if it is the fact that the Dominion has the right to the water powers on this navigable river, no matter how it may be impeded by rapids or rocks, it should be very jealous to keep all these powers to itself. The Ontario Government is getting all the value of the immense water powers on the Niagara river where really the Dominion should have a large

share ol them. We have a great war debt to liquidate, and if we have an asset in these navigable rivers I think it should be jealously guarded.

I do not want to enter into this highly technical question, but, speaking offhand, I always understood that the only right we have as a Dominion in navigable waters is the right of navigation. It must not interfere with our right to navigate those waters. In other respects, as I understand, the property belongs to the province.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Perhaps the hon. gentleman's idea is right, but I think he expresses it too strongly. The Dominion has full jurisdiction in respect of navigation. But assuming that the province has full ownership in respect of power, there is this difference between the rights of the two authorities: the right of the Dominion is paramount to all rights of the province in respect of power. That applies peculiarly to this river. The Niagara river is somewhat different; it is an international stream in respect of power. I am not asserting that the Dominion has no more right to power in Niagara that it has in the English river or in the Winnipeg river. There may be a difference in that regard; we do not need to argue it now. But so far as the Winnipeg river and the English river are concerned, both being navigable streams, the right of the Dominion to control for the purposes of navigation-the Dominion being the sole judge as to what are the purposes of navigation-is primary and paramount, and exercisable no matter how it may interfere with provincial properties as respects' water-powers. There is that difference; ours is first, theirs is second. This legislation takes away in no wise from either Dominion or provincial jurisdiction of either; it simply provides a mechanism for conferences in order that the respective jurisdictions of each may be exercised to the best advantage.
Has the minister considered what would be the effect of this provision on the power in question if the Federal Government should ultimately be found to be the owner of the power?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not see how that
could affect the question. The Dominion cannot by any act of its own either add to or substraet from its jurisdiction.
We have given the Ontario Government power to take a plebiscite on the liquor question formerly an exclusively federal matter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, the hon. gentleman's view of that is wrong. Certain jurisdiction and authority is given to the Dominion by the British North America Act; to that we cannot add and from it we cannot subtract, whether in regard te liquor or in regard to water. This legislation, therefore, will not have the least effect upon any judgment that may ultimately be given as to the real residency of the authority in respect to water-power.

The hon. member for
Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) has said that the Ontario Government is contemplating giving the power rights in the Winnipeg river to E. W. Backus, who, I understand represents very large interests. In my view, that would be the exercising of a control outside the power of the province. If the Dominion has the right to grant water-power rights in the Winnipeg river, those rights should be very closely guarded.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We are not at the
moment asserting any right to grant waterpower rights in the Winnipeg river. We are merely saying that rights granted in respect of water-power by the province must be subject to the paramount right of the Dominion in respect of navigation. Mr. Backus, or the Keewatin Power Company, owns the Norman dam, the key to the control of the levels of the Lake of the Woods but as that control is incident to navigation, Mr. Backus can have no rights in respect of the Norman dam except subject to the paramount rights of the Dominion in respect of navigation.

The particular instance
cited by my hon. friend was a lease of the power of the White Dog rapids on the Winnipeg river which he said was about to be granted. That is something that we should be very careful about. Of course the question is not now directly before us, but it may become very important. Such questions have gone to the Privy Council over and over again, and if at any time it should come to the fore and the Dominion should be found to be lax in the protection of Dominion rights, we should be prejudiced if we took any position here which would interfere with our making a stubborn fight in the future.

I understand that the
level of the Lake of the Woods is subject to international control. I cannot follow my

right hon. friend, therefore, when he states that the control of the levels of that lake is at present under the Dominion of Mr. Backus.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I explained that the
other day when requested to do so by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. 10 p.m. Murphy). The finding of the International Joint Commission is this: as the interest of the United States is an interest in respect of navigation, and as navigation is adequately taken care of if the levels are maintained between 1056 and 1061, it follows that while they are so maintained the United States does not need to come in at all; consequently the control between those levels is Canadian. The commission advise the creation of a board, the Lake of the Woods Control Board, to control the whole matter so long as they keep the high level at 1061 and the low level at 1056.
And it is between those two that Backus now controls?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It is between those two that it must be kept, and while so kept it is under Canadian control, but if it goes above 1061 on the one hand or below 1056 on the other the jurisdiction of a joint international board arises. All that this Bill says is that this board shall have control while the levels are maintained between the limits fixed by the International Joint Commission of between such other limits as the two countries may agree to-because we have not yet agreed on the report of the commission. When they go beyond the limits fixed, there is no board to act for the present, but if the commission's report is agreed to by the United States there will be an international board to take care of it.

What is the extent of
Mr. Backus' control now?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Backus really has no power to control. He is the owner, as I understand it, of the Keewatin Power Company which owns the Norman dam. The Norman dam controls the outlet of the Lake of the Woods and therefore the level of the Lake of the Woods, and Mr. Backus of the Keewatin Power Company has an agreement of many years' standing with the province of Ontario whereby Ontario exercises some authority over the Norman dam. But they have no power to exercise that authority; it is solely a Dominion authority, because it has to do with navigation and the Lake of the Woods. Now What we say is: follow out the reooimmenda-

tions of the International Joint Commission, in so far at least as they are not dissented from by the United States; pass this Bill and thereby establish a board which will be able to control, for the purposes both of navigation and of power, the levels of the Lake of the Woods. Its jurisdiction will be exercisable only if they keep the water between 1061 and 1056. That is all that we ask. The United States does not object to that. Therefore, the province of Ontario and the Dominion have come together, and they agree on this legislation in order that by this board the two jurisdictions may be exercised by Ontario and by the Dominion in conjunction and to the best advantage of both.
The board cannot order Backus, for instance, to raise or lower the level of the dam.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: It takes away that power, or rather it asserts on our part that he never had it.

The Prime Minister's explanation is satisfactory so far as it goes, and I notice from the last clause of this Bill that it is only brought into effect by Order in Council. In the meantime these matters can be looked into; but it seems to me that before we finally conclude an arrangement with the province of Ontario, which seems to be rather keen on asserting its rights to water-powers on navigable rivers, as the Dominion has rather let go its powers in the past, there should be a perfect understanding that this agreement is without prejudice to any rights that belong to the Dominion over navigable waters and water-powers that exist in navigable waters. As regard the St. Lawrence, I do not think anybody can say otherwise than that there is a dispute between the Dominion and the province. The province asserts its rights to water-powers in the St. Lawrence for its hydro-electric system. It is true that it is an international river, but I do not see that the principle is different. The Dominion is also asserting its right to those powers which are of enormous value. If the province is about to grant to a private person the water-power rights in the Winnipeg river, as is said by my right hon. friend, it may do so in other cases wherever there are rapids. Nothing should be done without the Dominion interest being protected in this respect.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.

On section 6,-enforcement of orders by taking possession of property.

Has the Prime Minister given any consideration to the reasonableness of allowing any compensation for taking over the dam? This dam has been built for the purpose of general navigation. The request came from the United States to have better water, and in some way or another-I do not now know why it was that Ontario had to do with the matter- the dam was built by agreement with Ontario at a cost of several hundred thousand dollars. The dam is for the benefit of all the powers on that lake. If it is to be taken control of absolutely, to the detriment of the owners, no matter whether it was built without the absolute concurrence of the Dominion Government and the expenditure having been made and the dam being in use, the owners ought to have some reasonable opportunity, whatever it may be, to make a claim for whatever is proper in the way of compensation. I would like it to be understood that, in raising this protest, I *am not holding any brief for any of the parties; but I want to see the Bill as fair as possible, and a provision should be inserted so that reasonable compensation may be given in cases where we override the ordinary common law and by this legislation step in and take something from any person or corporation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Firstly, I do not think this Bill is any step at all in the direction of confiscating or abolishing a claim for compensation; if any just claim exists, I think it could be established after the Bill passes, just as well as before. But at the same time, I want to say this, secondly, that in respect of a structure that interferes with navigation, in respect of a structure erected or existing in defiance of the Navigable Waters Protection Act, a Dominion statute whose provisions are unimpaired by this legislation, it does not seem to me that there is any claim for compensation.

Supposing to-morrow
the dam is blown out or washed out, we as a Government would have to rebuild it, would we not? Therefore, if we make use of it, should we not do something in the way of compensation?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is another question. But if a party erects, in a navigable stream, an obstruction and if it is found afterwards necessary to remove that abstruction or to impair its value, that
party, in my opinion as now advised, cannot make a claim for compensation. I do not remember the name of the case, but in the Chandler water-power case, tried in the Supreme Court of the United States, the verdict was to this effect, that as a power structure affecting navigation had been erected at the American Soo, and as it was necessary wholly to remove that structure for the purposes of the navigation of the Soo, although the company owned for the purposes of the power, the bed of the river, the riparian right and all, they had no claim whatever for compensation. Compensation to the extent, I think, of half a million dollars was given to them by the trial courts, but the Supreme Court of the United States reversed the decision and held that there was no claim. As at present advised, I am of opinion that any claim in connection with the Norman dam would be on all fours with that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If the Norman dam is used for Dominion purposes, then there may be a claim for compensation, having regard to its value; but if such a claim exists, this Bill does not take it away.
I want that made perfectly clear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: At the same time, I want to emphasize the fact that, with a Navigable Waters Protection Act existing, asserting and providing for the administration of the rights of this Dominion as regards navigation, as this dam is built, not primarily to control the level of the lake of the Woods, but for the purpose of the development of power, I do not think there is a very strong claim for compensation on the part of the owners of the dam; that is, unless property which is theirs is used for Dominion purposes and is on that account of no use to the owners of the property. In any event, all I need to say at this point is that, whatever rights they have, it seems to me they will be just as good after this Bill passes as before.
Does this last clause not confer power upon the commission to take possession of mills, dams and other obstructions?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Supposing, in taking possession, they break up the dam, they are doing it by right of this statute, and that puts an end to the right of any court to give the owners compensation unless compensation is provided for. When the owners got into court, the defence would be raised, that what was done was done by virtue of a statute, and the court would say: "There are no damages." If we are to give extraordinary powers to this commission to go in and take possession, for the general good, of a man's property,'in whatever shape it may be, there should be some provision to compensate that man for impairment done to his property.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is not what the hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora (Mr. Keefer) is asking for. I think he agrees -that if this is an obstruction to navigation which, in the judgment of the Dominion authorities, must be removed, there is no claim for compensation, because the man never had any right to put the obstruction there. That was decided in the Chandler case in the Supreme Court of the United States. All that the hon. member for Port Arthur and Kenora is asking for is that, if instead of this being an obstruction, it is of real use in the control of the level of the water, and we go in and use it, we should pay something for it, and that if we did not do so, we would have to build another to use in its place.
