If this man has a claim, the door is not barred by this legislation. Whatever rights he has now, he would have still.

What is the purpose
of giving this power to a body to go in and take possession of dams and other structures as they may think proper? That is conferring a new power which does not exist until this Act is passed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: For the reason that they must have it to be able to carry out their duties. The Government has this power to-day, under the Navigable Waters Protection Act. Under that Act the Dominion can take the Norman dam and clean it out from the bottom to the top, and pay no compensation whatever. All that this Act does is to confer that power which is ours upon the board, subject, of course, to such conditions as the Act imposes.

This particular clause gives power to go in and take over that dam-to take it, and use it. As a matter of fact, anyone with local knowledge of

the situation knows that the dam must always be kept as a regulating dam, and that if the dam was taken out you would have to put another one in. It cannot be used for the purposes of a power plant. It is perfectly clear that the operation of that dam will have to be taken into the government's hands. It is essential in the international interests, and for the cotrol of the water powers that are there, but it is unfair to take and use that dam and allow no compensation for it. That is the point I want to make.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: That is quite a different point from that taken by the hon. member for North Cape Breton and Victoria. I see the force of it, but I do not think the hon. member would argue that the passing of this Bill has anything to do with the question of compensation. I do not sge why there would not be the same power to compensate even though the Bill passes. There would be the same power to compensate as there is to-day. There would have to be an estimate introduced in the House, and it would have to be approved by Parliament.

We are giving power
under this clause to step in and take the dam and use it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We have that power
to-day. All we do by this Bill is to delegate that power. We could send our officer out to-morrow.
But you would have to compensate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: If we would have to, we would have to to-day. We do not take away any rights that now exist in that respect.

Our position as a legislative body is entirely different from that of a court. A court has to administer the law as it finds it. It might be obliged to *say that a man had a very fine piece of property, but that as far as the court was concerned, it could not allow him any compensation at all. We are in a different position. The man has built this dam I understand under the authority of a license granted by the province of Ontario. The province was acting by right of the Crown in the right of the province, and this man built his dam in good faith. Everything was perfectly in order. Possibly the dam was built before Confederation, I do not know; at all events, it was built in compliance with the conditions that then existed, and under the authority of the Gov-

ernment, who thought they had power to allow him to do that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: But they had not.

The man built the dam in good faith. Now we are proposing to change the conditions. Does anybody say that it would be fair, after this man had built the dam in compliance with the conditions imposed, and had operated it in good faith for many years, that just because the general interests of the country required it, we should step in and take that dam and give him no compensation at all?
I do not think it would be the big thing for Canada to step in and destroy a man's property, which he had built in good faith, and say to him: We have the right to take that away, and you get nothing for it. I do not think that is how we should act.

I do not think it is the intention of this legislation to take this dam away from the man, but rather to exercise the right to regulate the flow of water in accordance with the treaty arrangement between this country and the United States. The question of compensation is one that has not been clearly explained as yet to the House. The position taken by the hon. member for Port Arthur is that the legislation should provide for compensation in the event of the dam being taken over at any time in the future. This House does not legislate to cover remote contingencies of that kind. We are not here to legislate with regard to anything that may happen 20 or 25 years from now. The hon. member for Port Arthur is trying to have inserted in this legislation the basis of a claim, which the parties who own the dam would immediately try to enforce. For that reason, I think the best thing we can do is to pass the Bill as drafted, and leave alone this question of compensation which may arise in the future. The international commission which was established to regulate waterways and navigation along the international boundary, in the course of their examination of matters pertaining to the Lake of the Woods ascertained that a man had built a dam at the outlet of the lake. That dam might be used to flood the surrounding lands; there might be excess water there, or the man might let all the water away, and then there would be no navigation at all. I think this very same matter was the subject of a tremendous fight between the Ontario Government and the Dominion Government, as to who controlled the outlet
of the lake. For these reasons I do not think it would be wise to insert in the legislation anything that would make it possible for the parties interested in the dam to turn around in six months or a year and say: The Government will have to take over this dam, and pay me a couple of million dollars to regulate it. This legislation only re-as-serts the right of the Government, and turns the matter of the regulation of the dam over to a hoard which it names. I think we ought to pass the legislation as drafted, without inserting any regulations pertaining to compensation.

Of course, I am not so familiar as my hon. friend from Port Arthur with the local situation. I take it for granted, however, that this dam and the land there belong to this man, Backus. Now we have an Expropriation Act, which provides for compensation where land is expropriated. The Expropriation Act provides what steps shall be taken to ascertain the value of the property. Why is there any necessity for bringing in new legislation of this kind? There seem to be new powers taken here in addition to the powers of expropriation.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 8-Immunity from actions.

Just at this stage, before this section is carried, would it not be well, unless there is some general law covering the matter, to have a clause in the Bill providing that the Board shall make a report annually within a certain number of days after the opening of the session in order that Parliament might keep a check on that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I see no objection to that suggestion except that this is concurrent legislation and I do not like including an amendment that has not been agreed upon. The two amendments I have suggested have been agreed to by the Premier of Ontario. There is no doubt the board will make a report; they do through the department regularly. I would not object to the suggestion of the hon. member, but I should not like to include in the Bill anything that was not agreed upon.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: When shall the Bill be read the third time?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
At the next sitting.



House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
Miscellaneous-To provide for Canada's contribution towards the maintenance of the permanent Secretariat of the League of Nations, $200,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Perhaps my right hon. friend will explain how Canada's contribution has been arranged for?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The contribution last year was $200,000 and this year the same amount is asked for. The original basis of computation and distribution of the expenses of the League, as agreed upon, was the Universal Postal Union's basis, which placed Canada in the same rank as a first-class power and fixed its share on that dimension. At the last meeting of the League, a financial committee was appointed to consider the whole subject of the budget of the League and its- distribution, and one of the Canadian representatives, the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), was, I believe, the most active member of the committee. The committee made a report, and I understand it is quite confidently expected that as a result thereof a new basis of distribution will be arrived at. I think it would be well, in order to save time, for the Minister of Trade and Commerce, or the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Rowell), who is equally familiar with the situation, to explain the finances of the committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Let them
toss a coin to see who shall speak.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Or the Minister of Justice.

Since the others are bashful, and I am not, I suppose I may take it upon myself to make the explanation. Article 6 of the Covenant of the League arranges for the expenses of the League, and it adopted as the basis upon which the different members of the League should make their contributions the basis which had been adopted by the Universal Postal Union. The Universal Postal Union's expenses were limited to 125,000 francs, and that sum being very small, it made very little comparative difference as to whether the nations belonged to the first class or not. The Postal Union divided its national members into seven classes. The first class nations paid the largest amount and the lowest class the smallest; and in putting in their claims to be considered as first class or any other class nations, 
some of the smaller countries were ambitious and put in their names in the first rank. As I say, it made very little difference when the total amount to be allocated could not exceed 125,000 francs; that divided amongst twenty, or thirty or forty nations represented a very small sum for each one. When the basis of contribution was settled at the Peace Conference, after debating the question they decided upon the Universal Postal Union's basis of allocation and adopted it for the League of Nations. Consequently, the members of the League of Nations, based upon that allocation, took the same elass of nationality as they did in the Universal Postal Union. So it happened, to make it clear, that South Africa, for instance, that has a white population of only a million and a half, having been rated as a first class nation in the Universal Postal Union became rated as a first class nation in the League of Nations, and as the amount to be paid in the gross was very much more, the allocation attributed to her is exactly the same as is attributed to France, to Great Britain, and to the United States of America. Canada also elected to be called a first class nation in the Universal Postal Union and she, in the same way, on that basis of allocation, has to contribute as a first class nation. So you find South Africa and Canada-not to go any further-paying exactly the same amounts under that basis as those that are paid by the first class powers. Now that is manifestly unfair, but that basis of allocation was settled in the Treaty itself. It is in the Convenant, and it can only be rearranged and another basis adopted by an amendment of the constitution, so to speak. There is one other way in which it might be done. The Swiss Confederation at Geneva, which is the supervising authority of the Postal Union, may take up the basis of allocation for that Union, and may so arrange it that it will become a reasonable basis upon which the nations that belong to the League of Nations may make their contributions with fair and reasonable relation one to another. That is being sought to be done and a committee for the purpose was appointed at the first Assembly. That committee is working in connection with the Geneva supervising power to bring about, if possible, a change in the basis of allocation under the Universal Postal Union's basis for contribution. If that can be done and is satisfactory to the Council and to the League of Nations then the matter will be settled. If it cannot be

done then it has to be rearranged by the next Assembly which will meet in September. I do not myself believe that it will be possible before the first of July to make that arrangement with the Universal Postal Union. If that is not done the allocation this year to all the nations will be upon the same basis as last year's allocation, but it is agreed by resolution-which was introduced and passed in the committee and reported to the Assembly and approved by them-that the reasonable basis of allocation which shall be arranged and settled by the Assembly at its next session will be taken into account in the allocations made in 1921 and in 1922. The basis shall be the basis settled by the next Assembly and if Canada, for instance, now pays as a first class power an amount equal to what Great Britain pays, we will say, she will in 1922 have the allocation placed much lower compared with what it would have been under the past allocation and a country which has paid less than the allocation to be arranged for 1922 will pay more. So that as between the two years 1921 and 1922 the allocations will be upon a reasonable basis and the adjustments will be made in the way that I state. I think that is as clear an explanation as I can give.

The
right hon. gentleman told us that Canada was rated as a first class nation. Are all the nations in the League rated as first class nations?

I was speaking of the rating of the nations in the Universal Postal Union which was adopted as the, basis of contributions for the members of the League of Nations. Canada being rated as a first class nation in the Postal Union became thereby obliged to pay her contribution according to that rating.

My
right hon. friend admits that that basis is not satisfactory. Did that question come up at the time the matter was being dealt with, and if so was there any attempt to find a solution of the difficulty then?

The question certainly came up because it was settled in the Covenant at the Peace Conference. There had to be contributions and the question was on what basis those contributions were to be allocated. Different bases were discussed but it seemed then that the best way and the quickest way to settle it was to take what was agreed upon by the
nations in the Universal Postal Union. But when it came to be worked out the injustice of it began to be felt. So long as the contribution in toto was confined, as it is in the Universal Postal Union, it made so little difference that no nation felt there was a grievance.
I understand our contribution is two hundred thousand a year?
Yes.
We pay a pretty high price to be considered a first class nation.
Well, when it is rectified we will have the solace of paying a little less.
Could we demand a rebate or refund when we are put in class 2?
We obtain a rebate-yes.

I see that my hon. friend from Durham (Mr. Rowell) intends to address the Committee. Before he does so I would like to call attention to the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce the other night when he said that all this talk about a change of status, and so on, was good for young men like my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) and myself, but there was nothing to it. I would like to hear from the hon. member from Durham as to that, and learn whether he shares the opinion of the Minister of Trade and Commerce that all such talk is pure nonsence.

I do not want my hon. friend from Quebec East to mislead my young friend from Durham-I would not have that for the world. My hon. friends opposite were indulging in a little pleasant badinage at our expense and I made the mild suggestion that if it pleased them it did not hurt us, but to let it be confined to the younger and friskier members on that side of the House.
And my hon. friend from Durham is one of those "younger and friskier members".
But he is not on that side.
That is why the hon. member for Durham has resigned from the Government.

I was not going to address the committee, but rather to ask a question of the minister, and for the time being my hon. friend will perhaps pardon

my not answering his question. The minister will recall that a substantial amount in the Budget relates to the work of the technical organizations which have been established to carry out certain of-the functions of the league. He will further recall that at Geneva the assembly approved of the holding of a conference to consider certain international conventions relating to international transportation and communications. I understand that Canada was not represented at the Barcelona conference held in March. I do not know whether the Government has been advised of the decisions arrived at by that conference, and I am only speaking from the Times' report of the proceedings, but if that report be correct, it would appear that one of the steps taken was the creation of an organization relating to international communications and transit in the form of a technical advisory committee and body of delegates that would meet from time to time.' The question I wish to put to the minister is whether there was any discussion in the Finance Committee of the assembly as to limiting the costs of these technical organizations to the states that actually participate in them, or whether it was assumed that all states, members of the league, would contribute their quota?

I do not recollect the matter having been discussed along the line of a limitation of the expenses of any one of these technical organizations to the countries which would be chiefly benefited by them. I think the general line taken was that the expenses which were authorized should be met by the league as a whole. At the same time there was a limit as to the maximum expenditure, and the impression left on my mind was that as far as possible it should be kept within limits in order that the proposals and methods of work of these technical organizations might be reviewed by the assembly before they became permanent organizations and embarked upon more or less extensive operations. That I know with respect to three or four of them was absolutely made a part of the resolutions which were passed by the several commissions. The allocation of expenses is to be found in Article XIII of the resolutions which were passed first by the commissions and then reported to the assembly, and I find on looking at it that it is practically along the same lines as I have explained to the committee.

The reports of the Barcelona conference which have appeared in the Times rather lead one to the conclusion that in the absence of Canada the conference proceeded to do the very thing which at the instance of Canada the assembly decided not to do, namely, to set up a permanent organization to deal with international communications and transit. If this has been done, they have acted contrary to what I think we all agree was the decision of the assembly. One cannot but recognize that there may be real force in the argument that these permanent organizations are required to meet the needs of European countries, but it may be that upon giving the matter full consideration we will come to the conclusion, particularly if the United States should not enter the league, that we should not join in the conventions or take part in the organizations which have been recommended. I would draw the attention of the Government to the fact that at a meeting of the Council held during the latter part of 1920, when certain special committees were appointed to investigate particular matters, the question of whether the expenses of these special committees should be charged upon the general funds of the league or against the nations that were particularly interested in the work was discussed, and it was decided that in regard to the specific matters which they then had before them the expenses should be charged against the nations that were directly concerned. I would submit to the Government that this matter should be kept in view at the next assembly when the report is received from the Barcelona conference, and that if it should be decided that Canada should not join in the proposed conventions or be a party to these organizations, we should not be called upon to contribute to their expense but the expenses should be borne by the states that are pressing for their creation and will benefit from their activities.
I take this position because I am interested in the success of the league; I fear that if new organizations are set up to meet European conditions which involve a substantial increase in the general expense of the league, the non-European states will feel that they are being saddled with an unnecessary burden for the benefit of states and in respect of matters that are purely European. I simply want to direct the attention of the Government to the matter because it would appear from the press despatches that our friends who

gather together in that meeting proceeded to do the thing which the Assembly at Geneva, on Canada's instance, decided should not be done, namely, set up a permanent organization in connection with communications and transit.
My colleagues who were present at Geneva will recall the point that was taken by Canada in connection with all these technical organizations, namely, that the right to take action under article 23 of the covenant was predicted upon the existence of an international convention either already entered into or thereafter to be agreed upon. Some of the delegates present, I think, did not agree with that view. I submit, however, that it is only necessary to read the article to see the force of it. I gather that the Barcelona conference was proceeding to set up this organization without the existence of such a treaty or convention.
Was Canada represented at this Barcelona conference?
I understand that Canada had no representative there.
What was the purpose of the Barcelona conference?

It was called pursuant
to a decision of the Assembly to consider certain matters relating to international communication and transit. It was understood that there would be laid before this conference certain draft conventions which had been worked out by a committee on communications and transit for the consideration of the states, members of the league. There can be no question as to the importance of the gathering; no question as to the importance of the conventions. General , freedom of international communication undoubtedly is a desirable thing, both on land and on sea. But these conventions involve very substantial obligations upon the states that do enter into them to provide freedom of transit upon land and sea, so far as they control it, to international trade and traffic; and they set up a superior authority-that is, a technical committee which is to be constituted as part of the organization to determine questions in dispute. From that authority there may be an appeal to the Permanent Court of International Justice when established. Now, nothing has been done there which binds Canada unless we decide to assent to it. My point in regard to these matters is two-fold: first, in case Canada should decide not to assent, to the
conventions because having regard to our conditions we do not feel that we should enter into these conventions, then I do not feel it is right that we should be called upon to contribute towards the expenses on the same basis as states that are parties to these conventions. That is point number one. Number two is this: I think that for the sake of the future the Government of Canada should make its position quite clear that we do not think any organization can be created under Article 23 except under a convention entered into in accordance with the provisions of that article.
There is another point to which I wish to direct attention in the hope that the Government will take it up with the council of the league. It relates to the question of mandates, a matter on which the Minister of Justice is specially informed and in which he took a very special interest at the Assembly. I am sure every member of the House will most heartily con. cur in the statement he made
11 p.m. of Canada's position in the Assembly in reference to these mandates. But at that time we did not have the mandates before us. The council, for reasons which seemed to it good, did not submit the mandates to the Assembly. It was therefore impossible to make any suggestions at the Assembly in regard to the form of the mandates. The mandates have now been published in the London Times and have been the subject of debate in the British House of Commons. They are, therefore, public property, and it is consequently open to any one to make comment or suggestion with regard to them. I concur in the view presented by the Minister of Justice that the world may judge of the good faith of the Council of the league and of the nations who are mandatories by the spirit in which they carry out the trust expressed in the mandates and the covenant of the league. I wish to point out in my humble judgment the form of the mandates as published in the Times for the Central African group is not in accordance with the terms of the covenant in one important respect. Article 22 deals with the mandates. The first clause is:
To those colonies and territories which as a consequence of the late war have ceased to be under the sovereignty of the states which formerly governed them and which are inhabited by peoples not yet able to stand by themselves under the strenuous conditions of the modern world, there should be applied the principle that the well-being and development of such peoples form a sacred trust of civilization and that securities for the performance of this trust should be embodied in this Covenant.

Provision is then made for the appointment of the mandatories of it is declared that this tutelage should be exercised by them as mandatories on behalf of the League." As a member of the League we are necessarily interested in the matter. This is the provision in reference to the Central African group:
Other peoples, especially those of Central Africa, are at such a stage that the Mandatory must he responsible for the administration of the territory under conditions which will guarantee freedom of conscience and religion, subject only to the maintenance of public order and morals, the prohibition of abuses such as the slave trade, the arms traffic and the liquor traffic, and the prevention of the establishment of fortifications of military and naval bases, etc.
These provisions also apply to the C mandates, which cover the islands in the Pacific. The C mandates were issued and published while we were at Geneva. These mandates/ contain provisions prohibiting the slave trade and the liquor traffic so far as it relates to the natives residing in the territories. But when we come to the B mandates, those relating to Central Africa, in respect of which there is this express provision in the Covenant, the mandates provide for the regulation rather than the prohibition of the liquor traffic; they prohibit the slave trade but simply regulate the liquor traffic.
May I draw to the attention of the Government what was stated in the British House of Commons, viz: That Germany derived a substantial part of her revenue in administering East Africa by the sale of gin to the natives, and it was asked if it was contemplated that part of the revenue for the administration of this territory should be secured in that way. I am not at present concerned with the question whether the provision in the Covenant is wise or unwise, although I take it that the best authorities are agreed that the sale of intoxicating liquor among the native races is wrong and should be prohibited. But I say, in respect of this particular matter, where there is the express provision in the Covenant that the traffic should be prohibited, there is no justification for departing from the terms of the Covenant. As we are interested in the matter and it is now before the Council of the League, the Government, if it agrees with the view I have presented-and it is for the Government to consider that- should draw to the attention of the Council that, in our view, the mandate is not in accordance with the terms of the Covenant

and that, before it is approved by the Council, it should be brought into harmony with the terms of the Covenant.

As one of the very few that are not enthusiastic with regard to the League of Nations, I want to make one or two observations while the Estimates for the League are under discussion. I agree with a remark that was made from the other side a moment ago, and I think the hon. member for Durham also agreed with it, that we should not go into this in a financial way to too great a degree at the present time. It appears to me that the salaries that have been mentioned in connection with members of the League are out of all proportion to those that should be paid to men of such high ideals as are expressed with regard to the League of Nations. A list furnished to the House a few days ago shows that these gentlemen get from $15,000 to $40,000 apiece per annum, and such salaries appear to me, in times like these and in an idealistic cause, to be in excess of what is required for the work. This country is trying to be of a saving turn at the present time.
Personally, I do not look upon the League of Nations as an immediate asset to this country. I may be wrong; I know the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) thinks that it will stop all military expenditure; but I am not a believer in that, nor do I think in its present chaotic shape, it should * stop military expenditure by a single dollar, because the League of Nations is at present no bulwark with regard to the peace of the world. Wars are raging in many countries, and only to-night we read in the Montreal Star that Britain has sent a strong protest to Italy with regard to her co-operation with Turkey against Greece, in connection with contentions that have arisen as regards the possession of certain territory. If that is correct, it only goes to show that the League of Nations, while it probably represents one of the highest ideals that has ever been launched, is at present in a very academic state; it has not been able to function up to the present so far as keeping the peace of the vcorld is concerned, and I would be very sorry to see my good friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) carried away too much with the idea that the League of Nations is going to be, in the immediate future, a settlement of the wrongs of the world. For myself I cannot see that that will be the case. The ideal, as I have said, as propounded by ex-

President Wilson, was no doubt a very fine theory; but I am one of those who believe that all good ends have to be accomplished by the divine right and the divine law that have been laid down from the foundation of the world up to the present time as the guide for men and for nations.
I understand that the constitution of the League of Nations will more or less sap the vitality of our loyalty to our own country and Empire, and to all the countries and all the empires that are concerned in that great body. I cannot see that a super-force set up to rule the world can have the loyalty of all given to it in an unqualified sense, and at the same time that we should retain all the loyalty that we originally had in connection with our own country and Empire. I foresee that, while the League of Nations may succeed in drawing a certain amount of loyalty to itself, that will be more or less at the expense of the diminution of our loyalty to our own country and Empire. That is a consummation that I cannot view with equanimity. I have always relied upon the Minister of Trade and Commerce as being one of the pillars of the Empire. I hope that this vision that has come to him in these late days will not wean him away from loyalty to the old Empire that.he has supported so well and in which support we have been so proud to follow him. I do not say this in a jocular sense; I mean what I say in that respect. There is a real danger, and I cannot contemplate our giving our loyalty to that League if it is going to sap our loyalty to our own institutions, our country and our Empire.
Internationality is not a new idea. I heard the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) defining a Canadian national lately, and that has been one of the outcomes of the League of Nations. But the idea of having all the world composing one nation is not new. It is a very old idea; it was tried out some 6,000 years ago, and I would like to refer my good friend from Durham (Mr. Rowell) particularly to the eleventh chapter of the book of Genesis. I hope he will read the first fifteen verses of that chapter, where he will see what came to the world when the world was all one nation and all men of the world were speaking one language.
What is the reference? I want to look it up.

The eleventh chapter of Genesis, the first fifteen verses. I know that one of the patriarchs is speaking to me, but I thought he would know the book of Genesis as well as myself. In another discussion this evening he told us that he came from a race of prophets.
I am merely a descendant of the patriarchs.

The eleventh chapter of Genesis sets out what was the fact in the early days. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, a few weeks ago, told us that the nations of the world came together in that League speaking 47 different languages, if I remember aright, and that they went away speaking two. That is a consummation, perhaps, devoutly to be wished, but difficulties may arise when all speak one language. Read that eleventh chapter of Genesis to which I have referred, and you will see that the Lord God Almighty Himself came down to earth in order to see what all the people were doing. They were all speaking one language, and they were all apparently actuated by one idea. What did the Lord find they were doing? We are told that when He came down to earth, He found that they were building a tower of Babel which was to reach unto heaven and by which high tower they would get a short cut from earth to heaven. In other words they were going to attain a spiritual end by material means. The Lord did not approve that. What did He do? He did not send them away speaking one language; but He turned them into chaos by having them speak forty-seven languages in the way the minister told us that the representatives of these nations did when they came to the conference in Europe. These men of old came to build the Tower of Babel, speaking all one tongue, and the Lord was so displeased with them that he said: I want this work stopped, and the way to stop it, is to give the people different tongues so they will not understand one another. And he did so, and from that day on the people were scattered among the countries of the world, each people speaking a different language. So we have pretty high authority for this desire that many nations should exist in the world.
I cannot conceive that we shall find any short-cut to the millennium by bringing all the nations of the world to speak one tongue, or to be called one common people to-day. It is true the scriptures tell us in different places that all people are of one blood and one flesh, and all that, but the fact remains that the nations of the earth were created out of one nation by the will

of the Almighty, because they were attaining spiritual ends by material means and this is being done to a very great extent in many walks of life in a way that should not be. There is no short-cut to the millennium. It is the old good way of living, the spiritual life, and the implanting in the heart of man of good desires and right inclinations, that is going to make him good, and if you are going to make the nations of the earth good, you must build on the old foundation of the scriptures and the doctrines that are taught there. That will be the surest, if not the quickest, road to the millennium.
Therefore, I say that with this League of Nations Canada wants to go fairly slow. I do not want to ask Canada to withdraw from the League, but it appears to me, if the cables brought us correct reports of what the League of Nations did at its last meeting, we were put into a comparatively false position, because Canada appeared to be the king-pin of the whole League. There was more space given to the Dominion of Canada than to all the rest of the nations of the world put together. Now that is out of all proportion to our importance, as anybody can see. It is out of all proportion to our population, and out of all proportion to our means in every respect. While it is well to be always forward in good works, it is not well to take up such an advanced a position that you have not the material strength to maintain it later.
Is there anything in the scriptures which would be against Canada assuming the position she did assume then?

That is rather a
broad and leading question. I cannot say that I know all the verses in the scriptures, but my hon. friend form North Perth, (Mr. Morphy) reminds me that there is a text that runs: He that humbles himself shall be exalted.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That is how we came to be exalted.

I think it would be better if Canada had humbled herself a bit, and not, immediately the League met, begun to take the leading part among these 47 nations. There may be some nations that know something, and that have power, armies and navies, and that will be able to carry out the mandates of the League when all diplomatic endeavours have come to an end, because I understand that in the last resort there is the appeal to the big

stick, as there always has been, and always likely will be in this world; I cannot see it in any other way. Therefore, I say it is not desirable, to say the least, that Canada should place herself in the front rank of the nations of the world in this particular movement. Nearly all of these 47 nations are more populous than ourselves, and have greater material and financial resources, while man for man they may not be equal to this Dominion. I am willing to admit that the three gentlemen sitting in the front benches tonight were probably the three brightest men at the League of Nations-yet I think my hon. friends themselves will be the first to say that, with their usual modesty, the old tiger of Europe should have a little to say about the matter. It does appear to me that Canada was too prominent in the carrying on of the business of the League at its last meeting. I do not want to throw any cold water upon the efforts of the Canadian representatives.
Hot water, just now.

I do not want to be too critical. I am confident that they represented Canada to the best of their ability. I am glad to know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce has told the committee to-night that the status of Canada has not been materially changed. I did not hear him make the remark myself, but I heard an hon. gentleman on the other side attribute it to him, and as the minister did not disclaim it, I presume that he made it.
You must be very careful in accepting a statement that way.

I know I can hardly rely on quotations from the other side of the House as to what hon. gentlemen on this side say, but as the minister did not deny it, I thought I was justified in accepting it as correct. I did not want to see any change in the status of Canada at the present time. I do not think we have anything to grumble about, and I think it would be a very inopportune time now for Canada to allow any expression of discontent with her position to be sent overseas to Great Britain, which is almost submerged under the tremendous problem of straightening things out after the war.
I have in my hand an article upon a book recently written by the Right Hon.
J.	H. Thomas, entitled "When Labour Rules." Mr. Thomas foreshadows that the

League of Nations is not going to last as a League of Nations. He says that it must be immediately changed to a league of peoples; he draws a distinction between nations and peoples, and he states in his book what is going to happen when Labour rules, presumably in Great Britain. Labour is going to change the whole foreign policy; there are going to be no more treaties made and put in pigeon holes, he says; nothing of that kind will be allowed, but labour will go in for broad internationalism. I believe that there is a first, second, and third international; I do not know whether there are more, but I have seen the third international quoted very frequently lately, so I presume there must be a first and second. But all of these are very much untried experiments, and I would urge my hon. friends on the front bench when they go across to the league next time to be extremely cautious in taking up any advanced position with regard to what Canada is going to do in the League of Nations.
There was one suggestion made, I believe, by the Minister of Justice, a gentleman for whom I have the profoundest respect, for which I do not know whether he had a mandate. If the despatches can be' believed, the Minister of Justice was responsible for the request that Article 10 be removed from the constitution of the League of Nations. Now President Wilson, who perhaps had more to do with the formation of the league than any other one man, said that Article 10 was the backbone of the whole league. Article 10 is the crux of the whole thing. When other means fail, resort can be had to Article 10, which calls upon every nation that is a member of the league to contribute its share of armed forces. I think hon. members will agree that Article 10 is therefore a very substantial entity in the League of Nations, and I question very much the wisdom both from our standpoint and that of the British Empire, of having it removed from the constitution of the league at the present time. I am only a humble layman and cannot hope that my judgment will be accepted for a moment alongside that of the Minister of Justice, who has had a great deal more experience with world affairs than I have, but to make very drastic changes in what we have been told is almost a divine law, to cut out the heart of it so to speak, or, if you prefer to put it another way, to break the backbone of the league and
make it inoperative under certain conditions, is something I cannot view with equanimity. I think it would be well for us to wait until we see whether the nations of the world can live up to the high ideals that are propounded by the league.
The League of Nations is supposed to be a part of the Treaty of Peace. All our discussions, however, have concerned themselves with the League of Nations, and I have heard scarcely a word about the Treaty itself. The Treaty of Peace seems to have been submerged and lost sight of entirely in an ideal that it is supposed is going to work wonders in the future, although it apparently takes no cognizance of what has been done in the past. The primary object of the whole undertaking, in the first place, was to make a treaty ot Peace. When our delegates went from this country over to Europe I understood that their mission was to take part in the framing of a Treaty of Peace, which, of course, was a very desirable thing after a war of the kind we had experienced. It therefore seems strange to me that the Peace Treaty should be lost sight of and that we should, to all intents and purposes, lose practically the whole result of our efforts, in some panacea which is intended to cure all the ills of the future. As I see the situation, we have lost our chance of getting any reparation, indemnity, or anything else, and if the only result of the whole affair is some universal remedy to be applied in the future, without any provision for the ills that should be repaired at this present moment, then I say that we are being robbed. of everything for which we fought and for which the world was drenched in blood. The Treaty of Peace is a matter of profound interest to all the nations that were concerned in the war, but we find to-day that the victors are, if anything, suffering more than the losers; they are taxing themselves to death, bleeding themselves white, to pay for a war that was brought on by an enemy who should be made to pay the piper, so far as they are able to do so. The Treaty of Peace, apparently, does not engage the attention of the League of Nations to any extent, so far as I have been able to judge; at all events, I do not see that many beneficial results will accrue to us by reason of it.
The situation appears to me in this way: We had a tremendous conflagration in the world, against which we held certain insurance, and we deputed certain delegates from Canada, as was done by the Empire generally, and all the other interested



nations, to meet and make a settlement with the people who had caused the damage; and when the report is brought back, when the Treaty of Peace and the Covenant of the League of Nations are presented to us, we find that the insurance policy which we thought was so good is of no avail, the money is not going to be paid, and we are. not to be indemnified. I saw the statement the other day that Britain is not going to receive one shilling in the pound for the losses she sustained in the war. It appears that these representatives, for whom, as I say, I have the profoundest respect, because they no doubt were unable to do anything, although they did not tell us so, instead of bringing back anything substantial in the way of results from the Peace Conference, bring us back a panacea that is going to cure all the ills of the future without making the slightest attempt to secure reparation for the ills we have already suffered through the fault of others. In other words, the insurance is not collected; the buildings have to be reconstructed, and we have to foot the loss.
The panacea proposed to us is this: If you build concrete, steel, iron and other non-combustible structures, you will have buildings that will last against fire for all time. That is practically the proposition that is put up to us. Now, we knew that before; we were perfectly aware, before ever we were told anything about the deliberations of the Peace Conference, that if we built with indestructible materials our buildings would be fireproof, and that if we could possibly bring war to an end it would be a consummation devoutly fo be wished. But we settled the peace without getting results, and we have a remedy that may not prove efficacious in the future.
I hope I have not misinterpreted, nor said anything unkind of, any one, because I have the kindliest feeling towards all those gentlemen who represented us so ably; but I trust sincerely that we shall not run after a rainbow, be it ever so bright and alluring, or chase after a pot of gold in the shape of good resolutions and high ideals, without securing any material advantage to ourselves and the other nations that were concerned in the rack and ruin which this great world war has caused.
I certainly do not contemplate that I shall live to see the day when all the nations of the world will become one vast brotherhood and one people. I should like to see it.

When swords shall be
turned into ploughshares.

That certainly would be the millennium, but I do not expect it in my generation, nor in the near future, and I have no hesitation in saying that I do not think the League of Nations, even with its lofty ideals and aspirations, will bring us any nearer to that ideal. I believe that all good ends must be obtained by good means, and the good means are laid down, as rules, in the word of the Almighty Himself; and we feeble men upon the earth cannot upset, by any short-cut system, those foundation principles that have existed since the world was created. I hope we shall not lose sight of these things, and chase after what I fear will prove to be a disappointment to all those who place too much of their resources in this one basket. I say, therefore, on questions of finance and the expenditures of the League, and on the question of our taking up too advanced a position on idealistic proposals, we had better be very careful, not only on our own account, but lest we mislead others. I trust I have not said anything harsh about any one, and my hope is that these remarks will be accepted in the spirit of kindliness in which I have endeavoured to give them.

It was said of the late Lord Palmerston that he once attended a church on a certain Sunday and came out with expressions of considerable annoyance regarding the sermon. Why, said he, that preacher speaks as though religion were a matter for every day in the week. I must say that I was reminded of that anecdote after listening to the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Cockshutt.) Religion, it seems, is an excellent thing but it is far too idealistic, far too impracticable to be introduced into the world affairs or into any endeavour to get rid of wars. The divine law, according to the hon. member for Brantford, is to keep people apart, and to have them speak different languages. The destruction of the tower of Babel, according to him, if I understand correctly his theological references-and I have not had the early pulpit experience which he has had to enable him to do justice to the situation-was a punishment for people who were trying to speak a common language. According to my hon. friend, it is better to speak different languages; and I was therefore surprised, on inquiry of the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), to find that the hon. member for Brantford had voted against the Lapointe resolution which advocated the teaching of French in Ontario some years ago.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman would allow me-I do not think he wishes to misrepresent what I said. I did not say that it was a punishment on the nations because they all spoke one language; I said it was a punishment upon them because they were building the tower of Babel to get into Heaven. Instead of following in the scriptural way by implanting the grace of God in their hearts, they were trying to attain a spiritual end by material means.
I would have thought -and I speak with all reverence-that perhaps the words "Blessed are the peacemakers for they shall inherit the kingdom of Heaven*' should be our motto.
No, the true reading is "for they shall be called the children of God."

Do not misquote the
scriptures.
My hon. friend from Brome has not got it right.

However, I can take it as a motto for the men who after all, whether they are completely successful or not, are trying to develop a new world order. The old world order, of which the member for Brantford is such a splendid exponent, has proved itself a ghastly failure and a horrible mistake. Those who have trusted to the sword have sulfered through the sword; and although we may find, and no doubt will find, many faults in the organization of the League of Nations-doubtless we will be able to see many defects in it-I would think that all who had aspirations for the betterment of mankind could spend their time to better advantage than trying to depreciate the very idea of endeavouring to arrange some other system of settling international disputes than by the sacrifice of the youth of all nations such as we have seen in the last few years. I am afraid the hon. member who has just taken his seat has not quite realized the object of the League of Nations. As I understand it, the object is not to set up a super-state to overpower all other states. To the League of Nations the nations of the world will give that consideration and concurrence which any reasonable man gives to, let us say, the municipal organization under which he lives. It will not sap our loyalty. I am sure the member for Brantford is no less fond of those immediately near to him
because he has affection for the town which he represents, or the province in which he lives, or the Dominion under whose flag he exists. I am sure that does not lessen his affection for those nearest and dearest to him; and the appreciation of, and the devotion to, the great ideal which is found in the League of Nations will not sap people's individual patriotism for their respective countries, but will rather enhance it. After all there is something greater than the country we live in, there is something greater than the flag which flies over us, and that is the consideration we should have for the whole of humanity. The divine law is not that the people should be divided into hostile camps, one portion of humanity warring against another, but the divine law, I believe, is that we should recognize the universal brotherhood of man. The member who just took his seat was complaining that there had not been any reparations collected. Did the hon. member ever think that it would be possible to make Germany pay for the war?
Surely.

Some one says
"surely." I remember the Minister of Finance some years ago, Sir Thomas White-I can refer to him now by name because he is no longer a member of the House-stating in his Budget speech, I think in June, 1919, that in his calculation of Canada's financial position he was not considering the possibility of reparation. I think if Germany can be forced to repair the material damage done to France, and the material damage done to individuals who have suffered through the war-I believe if she can be forced to do that-and I understand she has offered to repair the damages in Northern France herself-I do not know whether we can expect to get, or whether we will ever get, very much more. I would remind the member for Brantford, who, after all, I think is one of the most distinguished and outstanding protectionists in this House, that a debtor nation can only pay an indemnity in goods, and I do not think that a more eloquent or more vociferous voice than his will be raised in this House against any proposal to allow the Canadian market to be flooded, as my hon. friend would express it, with German goods. And if you do not allow the goods of Germany, in payment for reparation, let us say, to come into your own market, they must find some neutral market where they will compete with the goods manufactured by Great Britain and

by other nations. As a matter of fact I do not think there is any other way in which reparations can be made unless Germany is allowed to go into France and to repair to some extent the material damage that she has caused.
What about payment in gold?
There is not in Germany a one-hundreth part of the gold to enable them to pay.
You are altogether mistaken.

I am not altogether mistaken. The trouble is that our protectionist friends have the idea that international commerce is carried on on the same principles as obtain in a corner grocery; they think that cash passes with every transaction. They do not seem to realize-although you would think their experience as business men would have taught them differently-that most international transactions-in fact most transactions of any size-are merely a question of bookkeeping, and that the cry of keeping your money at home is absolutely unsound in economies.
Would my hon. friend leave Belgium entirely out of the reparations and confine the payments to France? The hon. gentleman said that.

Oh, no, Sir, not for a moment. I alluded to France as an illustration. Of course, Belgium should receive the same treatment. I am sure the hon. member would not think I would desire to overlook Belgium. [DOT]
Does the hon. gentleman not know that the Belgium indemnities are to be paid in German bonds which are to be cashed by the United States?

I had not heard that, but unless the Yankee has lost his proverbial sharpness I should think they would be taken at a very considerable discount. However, that is not the principal question in regard to which I rose to my feet. I would endorse the words of the hon. member for Durham, and also the words of the hon. member for Brantford, that we should observe economy in every possible way, but I believe that the Government in this regard is quite in sympathy with the views which we are now expressing. I do not believe that the Minister of Trade and Commerce who so

long criticised-I will not say in harsh but certainly in energetic terms-the exepndi-tures of the Liberal Government between 1896 and 1911, would lay his economical principles altogether aside. The poet has said:
'Tis better to have loved and lost
Than never to have loved at all.
Hear, hear.

And those who have loved and not lost I am glad to see are most vociferous in applauding that sentiment. But, Mr. Chairman, it would be infinitely better for the honour of Canada and for the honour of humanity that we tried to make this League of Nations work, even if our attempts should fail, than not to have tried at all. But, after all, we are faced with this situation, are we not? The past organization of international society has proved an awful failure, it has brought humanity to a position where a great part of the civilized world is on the verge of bankruptcy and hei civilization is absolutely demoralized. Now. that being the case, is it not wise to give another organization of society a chance: It is true we need faith and we need1 cooperation, and it is true that there are many things to discourage us, but if the ideal is right it is worth while for a nation like Canada, which has some idealism in its make-up, to endeavour to do what it can to make this League a success.

Mr. Chairnrian, I do not think it is necessary for me to deal with the principle of the League of Na-. tions, for it has been accepted by every hon. member except my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt). I absolutely agree with my hon. friend from Durham that no part of the money contributed by Canada should go to defray the expenses of technical or other commissions in the proceedings of which we have no share and upon which we are not represented. The principle of no taxation without representation applies to the League of Nations as to any other constitutional body.
There is another question to which I wish to refer-the question mentioned by my hon. friend from Brantford. Of course, I absolutely disagree with him-
You always do.
-as to article X in the League of Nations Covenant. That is the only part of the covenant that my hon. friend is in love with, because the application of force is implied in that article.

Somebody else
thought so when he put it in.

When the Peace treaty was discussed in this House some of us on this side took a strong stand against Article X, and we were harshly criticized by our friends opposite and by the press supporting the Government. It was a surprise to many of us last summer to read that my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) had asked for the repeal of that article, and it was a greater surprise to learn that at the Peace Conference the right hon. member for King's, N.S., (Sir Robert Borden) who was then Prime Minister, opposed the article. Why should we have been kept in ignorance of that when the Peace treaty was under discussion in this House? Why was it that the policy of secrecy prevailed and we were not then told that our representatives were in accord with the views expressed on this side of the House? I desire to know exactly what view my right hon. friend the Minister of Justice expressed at the last assembly of the League with respect to Article X.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry that the hon. gentleman should be under the impression that there is any endeavour to withhold any information as to the position of the Government in respect to Article X or to the treaty as a whole. If the hon. gentleman will look at what was said on behalf of the Government when this House was asked to ratify the treaty, he will see in the first place that when the right hon. member for King's, N.S., then Prime Minister, introduced his resolution for the ratification of the treaty, he expressly pointed out that he did not ask the House to adopt that resolution-I do not pretend to give his exact words, but I am satisfied I am giving their substance - because the treaty was just the treaty that we would have made had we had the making of it all alone, nor because all the provisions of that treaty, taking each one by itself, was to be approved and commended, but that he submitted the treaty as being the result that had been achieved in face of the fact that you had to get the assent of all these various nations, which made it necessary for each one to accept something that differed from what it would have thought was the best provision possible. So much for the treaty in general.
With respect to Article X of the Covenant, if the hon. gentleman will do me the
honour to refer to the debate upon that same resolution, he will find that in so many words I expressly said that I did not contend that we ought to have assumed all of the obligations that were contained in Article X. I was dealing with an amendment proposed from the other side of the House. I did take the view, which I still entertain, that that article did not involve the danger that was sought to be guarded against by that particular amendment, and to that I addressed myself. When I ask the hon. gentleman to go through my speech, it is not a mere formal request. Not only did I make the statement to which I have already referred, but I repeated it in a different form, and when I asked the House to join with us in ratifying that Covenant, I pointed out precisely my reasons for doing so. Those reasons were, not that all of the provisions of the Covenant were such as I thought Canada ought permanently to adopt, but that among those provisions was one making it possible to amend that Covenant. What I asked the House to do-in as much as we were unanimously agreed, as the hon. gentleman has himself said, that the principle of the League of Nations was right-was not to reject the Covenant because at the first attempt to frame the constitution of that league success in our judgment had not been attained in every provision. I pointed out that what I still think is obviously true, that if Canada had then chosen, because she did not like Article X or did not like some other provision in that Covenant, to have said, "No, we will not ratify this Covenant," what the consequence would have been of such refusal. Our position in that regard differed very materially from the position of the United States; our adhesion had not the same importance for the League which the adhesion of the United States had. Notwithstanding the observations of my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) we did not claim at the Assembly of the League of Nations to represent the most powerful nation in the world. May I 12 m. point out to him the true and at the same time the scriptural explanation of how we came to be so greatly exalted there? The hon. gentleman pointed out that the scripture said that those who humbleth themselves should be exalted. Now, as to our being so highly exalted at Geneva, does he not find the explanation in the very text that he himself gave us? But that is only by way of

parenthesis. What I did point out to the House was that Canada, while she did not approve of certain provisions of the Covenant, was placed in the position where, if she believed in the principle and wanted improvements in particular provisions, her only course was to ratify them. If she failed to do so she was on the outside, voiceless and powerless to bring about any improvement. If she did so, then she placed herself within the League of Nations, and, as I pointed out then, entitled herself to representation in the forum where she could effectively appeal for amendment to the Government, for the disappearance of those clauses to which she objected, for the improvement of those clauses which she thought susceptible of improvement. Following that statement which I made to the House, when I found myself, as a consequence of the ratification by Parliament of the treaty, in the forum to which I had been looking forward, I proceeded on Canada's behalf to ask for what seemed to us the most important amendment called for by the Covenant.
Now, the hon. gentleman has asserted that we had opposed that clause in Paris. That is perfectly true; we did oppose it. The hon. member for King's (Sir Robert Borden) wrote a memorandum on the subject; I myself wrote some memoranda on it.
I do not know that I would be violating any confidence at this time if I said that we came within an ace of succeeding in Paris.
I think it is a fairly open secret to-day, if it ever was a secret, that the insertion of Article 10 was really the work of one great power. Now, I do not know that I can add anything further by way of explanation. I think that the hon. member for Quebec East and members of the House generally, if they will do me the honour of re-reading the speech in which I asked them to ratify the covenant, will see that I never represented to them that I was asking them to do it because I myself approved of every clause in that covenant. With regard to Article 10 in particular they will find my express declaration that I was not even prepared to say that we should be bound by or that we should ever have accepted the particular obligations involved in that article.
Now, it is not pertinent to the question that the hon. member asks me-and it would lead us, I think, into too long a discussion at this hour-if I were to enter into the reasons why I think that Article 10 should not have been included in the Covenant; why I thought at Geneva and 
still think it ought to be eliminated. Some other occasion may present itself for my doing so, if hon. gentlemen are interested in hearing the reasons. I believe that they are conclusive. They were looked upon as so conclusive that, as I have said, we came within an ace of succeeding in striking out Article 10 ( at Paris. While the motion which I made at Geneva for the elimination of Article 10 was not passed then and there, I may say that neither was any adverse opinion expressed with regard to it upon the substance of the motion itself. It shared the fate that befell all proposed amendments; that is to say, it was determined that before proceeding to amend the Covenant there should be careful study by a commission-I think we would call it a committee over here; at all events they called them "commissions" there; I believe there is a distinction between the French "commission" and our "committee"-there should be a careful study of the proposed amendments by a commission appointed by the Council, the fruit of that study to be placed before the next meetings of the Assembly and any action deemed necessary upon the proposed amendments to be taken at that time. I may venture to add this much: that I did not make my proposal without feeling my way a little and ascertaining something of the disposition of the greater and smaller powers upon the subject. Without going into the details, I must say that because of the strength of the reasons which may be invoked in support of the proposal and from the views expressed to me by representatives of different countries, I feel that we may look forward with confidence to bringing about that very great improvement in the Covenant, which, in my judgment at all events, would result from the elimination of Article 10. I should be glad to have an opportunity at some time to explain, particularly for the benefit of my hon. friend from Brantford, the reason why I entertin so different a view regarding Article 10 from that which he entertains. It look to me as if he misapprehends Article 10, its purpose and its effect. Of course, it may be I who misapprehend it. Apart from objections of a general nature there are very special objections relating to a country situated as ours is.
I did not intend to take up so much time, but I did think it was fair that I should answer the question put to me by the hon. member for Quebec East. I hope I have made it clear to him at all events that there was no intentional misleading on my part.

I am sure that if he will re-read my speech he will find that there is no inconsistency between what I said in that speech and the action which I took at Geneva; that on the contrary the action which I took at Geneva was the natural and logical outcome of the reasons for which I asked the House to ratify the Covenant.

It was suggested in the press during the Geneva conference last winter that the elimination of Article 10 from the treaty was mooted in order to obtain some success in inducing the United States to enter the League. Can the hon. gentleman tell us anything about that?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: That formed no part of the motive that brought about our making the proposal. The proposal was made carrying out the views, as I have said, which had been entertained by Canada's representatives from the time of the adoption of the Covenant. I am quite prepared to add that I have no doubt that all of the nations who formed part of the League of Nations would welcome with open arms the incoming of the United States. I think Canada would join in extending that welcome, and it would be an additional reason why we would feel that we had done good work in bringing about the elimination of that article, if we should succeed in bringing that about, if it should transpire that that elimination should prove to be an important factor in determining the United States to enter the League of Nations. But we made our motion at the time of its proposal in Paris, for the reasons which led us to object to the article, reasons based upon considerations of general interest and reasons based in a special way upon consideration to countries situated as our country is.

I do not wish to prolong the discussion, but I do not wish to allow the opportunity to pass because of some remarks made by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) with reference to the German indemnities. In the first place, the Germans signed a Treaty of Peace, by which they agreed to make certain pay* ments in gold, and that is an obligation on them which they have refused to carry out from the time they signed that treaty. They knew at that time whether they could pay in gold or in articles such as coal and one thing or another of that kind, but they certainly agreed to pay a certain amount of the indemnity in gold, and so far they have failed to do so. If the Germans would pay in gold that portion of the
indemnity which they agreed to pay in gold, the position of the Allies would be immediately relieved. The Allies owe the United States something like eleven billion dollars, on which no interest has been paid ever since the war started or since they got the loan. If the Germans paid up part even of the cash indemnity which they have already agreed to pay, the money would be handed over to the United States, and Great Britain, France, Belgium and the other nations would be relieved of the necessity of paying cash to the United States to that amount.
_ I think my hon. friend is wrong in saying that Great Britain has not paid her interest.

By agreement she has
not. I know that as a fact, because I was reading the statements made by the Secretary of the Treasury only last week. On a certain part of the loan, she has not paid any interest. France and Italy have not paid any. If Germany had paid her indemnity, the whole situation would be relieved. The mission of Yiviani to the United States a short time ago was for the purpose of discussing that question with the new United States Government, and the latter are recognizing the fairness of the proposition; they have stated distinctly that Germany must pay. Many hon. gentlemen, like the hon. member for Brome, have taken the position:	"Oh, let England
pay up to the United States and let the Germans off."

I must not allow the
hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Currie) to misinterpret my remarks or to misquote me in this House. I never suggested that the Germans should be let off paying. What I said was that the Germans, when they came to pay, would have to pay in goods; that that would cause great economic disturbance in the world and that I did not believe the Germans would be able to pay the indemnity placed upon them. I may be wrong. That is my idea.

The hon. gentleman is
trying to square himself.
Not a bit.

His attitude to the House was that he would squeal if the Germans had to pay, even in goods. As a matter of fact, there are three methods by which the Germans can pay. I would ask the hon. member for Brome to get a primer on political economy and learn something about business or at least, international

business. Germany can pay by goods. Of course, we could not absorb all those goods at once. She can pay by gold, which is the method by which international exchanges are balanced. She can pay by bonds and other securities. As a matter of fact, within the last two or three weeks, the announcement has been made that the Belgian indemnities are to ibe paid by German bonds which are to be handed over to the United States, and the United States agree to accept them and to finance Belgium. That was not generally known, but the fact has been made public. How did France pay her indemnity? She paid it partly out of the gold which the nation held; but she made an issue of bonds which were sold internationally, and from that she got the cash for the indemnity which was paid in 1870.
She had the credit.
Does my hon. friend think that this will be all right by May 1?

Yes. There is enough
money standing to the credit of Germans and Germany in the United States to pay one-half of the eleven billion dollars that they owe-

That would
be a great relief to us.

-and there is enough
gold in Germany to pay one-half the indemnity. The German bank statements will 
show that. The cry of the Germans that they are not able to pay is only an excuse which they have in order to try to build up their country as long as they can. While the Allies are bleeding, the Germans are holding their money; they are exploiting their workmen; they are running their factories full-steam, and they are in ten times better position than this country is to-day, just because they have not had to pay one cent. So much for that.
As regards the Germans paying in goods, I believe this country should put a surtax on German goods. The German workman is working for 24 cents a day, and thousands of them are glad to get work at that in their factories. Their factories are working overtime. In Canada, what are our factories doing? We have factories closed to-day that have not been closed for thirty years. -Why? If this country and Great Britain had been relieved by the payment of the indemnities in cash, the exchanges would have been straightened right away, and we and the Empire and everybody else would have been far better off. The trouble with business to-day is that Germany's promise to pay is no good. If she had not promised to pay-and I have in my hand the Treaty with her signature to it, and she is now breaking faith with everybody in the whole world-we might excuse her, if she said: "I will not agree to pay anything until I see how my business affairs are." Germany was not destroyed by the war; she carried on the war entirely herself on paper; she jdid not borrow gold from anybody, and she does not owe anybody except her own people. That is the situation in Germany. Unfortunately, owing to the fact that the United States did not come into the war at the same time as we did, large engagements were made with the United States for money for munitions, and now everybody owes everybody else. Great Britain owes us large sums of money to-day, which could be paid if the Germans would only pay up their gold.
How can everybody owe everybody else? Does my hon. friend mean that England owes France and France owes England?

France owes England.
Mr. CLARK How can everybody owe everybody else?

Perhaps not everybody everybody else. The hon. gentleman poses as one of the economic critics of this House,

and I think with his great knowledge he ought to know that France, Italy and all our European Allies owe Great Britain, and Great Britain owes to the United States. The ultimate debt owing to the Unied States is eleven billion dollars.
Now I understand.

As a matter of fact, the only nation that does not owe anything is the United States, but even she owes to her own people. The debt is carried by the people of the United States. That is owing, and will be paid.
So the United States won the war after all? They paid for it anyway.

They paid for it any way. The preposition that was advanced by the pro-German element who are anxious to get out of paying their fair share to relieve Germany was that the United States should relieve Great Britain and the Allies from the payment of their debt; in other words, tljat the United States should take over the debts and the indemnities the Germans should pay for this war. I glory in the spunk of the United States in not accepting that proposition. If they had accepted it, it would have meant that all the cost of the war would have been saddled on the United States taxpayers. I am very glad that the United States took the position they did and said that Germany must pay for the war. Germany has ample money and can get ample credit from the Allies, to pay for this war just the same as France paid for the war of 1870.
Another thing I wish to refer to is the position taken by our delegates at the last meeting of the League of Nations. It is extremely unfortunate that our delegates took the position they did. We had accepted the Treaty in this House, and many of us did not go to the trouble of even reading it. We accepted it because Great Britain, France, and our Allies had accepted it, and we accepted it just as any person will take charge from an honest grocer. After we had accepted it, we did not expect that our delegates, when they went over there, would take any other position than the pure British position. I certainly did not. The Covenant of the League of Nations is very clear. There is not a single paragraph in the Covenant that a boy in the fourth book in any public school cannot understand. It is couched in the most simple language. For centuries
efforts have been made to devise methods whereby nations could submit their disputes to arbitration.
