I unfortunately have not with me the speeches of Cobden and Palmerston, but my hon. friend from Red Deer is so well posted on these matters that he will recall that at on time Cobden introduced a resolution in the British House in favour of arbitration, and that on that occasion Palmerston made one of his greatest speeches. He said that the idea was splendid, that he quite agreed with the theory of arbitration, but the difficulty of the whole thing was that after you had had arbitration, what could you do if the nation that was found in the wrong would not accept the award? In any provision for arbitration he said, there must be a clause providing for the ultimate use of force. Now in the Covenant of the League of Nations every possible method was provided whereby the nations of the world could bring their disputes before a proper tribunal. Those of us who have been at war realize its horrors perhaps more vividly than those who have not. The fact is there is nothing so terrible as war, and for centuries nations and peoples have been anxious to find a way of avoiding war. When this last war, the greatest in the history of the world, was over the nations that had won decided to try and form a league to try and prevent war. They all agreed upon a Covenant, and signed Article 10, except the United States. Article 10 is very short. I will read it:
The Members of the League undertake to respect and preserve as against external aggression the territorial integrity and existing political independence of all Members of the League. In case of any such aggression or in case of any threat or danger of such aggression the Council shall advise upon the means by which this obligation shall be fulfilled.
What does that mean? It means, not aggression, but protection. It means that every nation that signed the covenant of the League, when its territory is threathened by any other nation, wiil have behind it all the other members of the League. What does that mean to us? We have a very long boundary. The United States has always been friendly, and we hope it always will be, but the United States would not stand for that clause, and they refused to accept the Treaty on account of it. The only country whose territory might be threatened would be ours; let us be frank about it. Japan has signed the Treaty, but suppose Japan got into trouble with the United States and undertook to occupy our territory. That

would be breaking the rules of the Covenant, because no member of the League can go to war with any other country within the League or outside until all the peaceful resources of the League have first been exhausted. But suppose Japan waived aside the League, went to war with the United States, and attempted to use Canada as a base. Under article 10 all the other nations of the League would immediately come to our assistance. Now what has happened in the United States? All the pro-Germans there, and all the journals and people opposed to Great Britain, made a great cry at the last election against the signing of article 10 by the United States. If the United States had accepted the Covenant there would be no question about the security of the League and all the things contained therein, but unfortunately the League was made a political question in the United States and it was defeated. I am satisfied, however, that the good sense of the United States sooner or later will come to the rescue, and that country become a member of the League. Now if the Covenant is going to be of any value, it should not be touched, to my mind, for at least 10 years. If no attempts are made to change it for that length of time it will stand, and we will have world peace for another 100 years. There is tio question about that. It will be the same as it was when Confederation was brought about. There was a whole lot of talk about changing this clause and that for a time, and it was made a matter of local politics as to what should be done, but fortunately the Fathers of Confederation and the people of Canada stood by that Act, with the result that it stands to-day, and will no doubt stand as long as the world endures.
I was one of those members who helped to ratify the treaty in this House, and much to our surprise we found that nearly all the nations began to amend the Covenant at that meeting of the League, instead of taking the position that, as the ink on the paper was hardly dry, they would wait at least for a while and see how the Covenant worked out. I say without hesitation that our representatives should have taken the position held by the British; they should have been absolutely behind Great Britain, because, whether Great Britain is right or wrong in international affairs, we have been always with her. The late Sir Wilfrid Laurier laid down the dictum that when Great Britain is at war Canada is at war, and that is the position 
we should take. I am one of those who never dreamed for a moment that our delegates, after having induced this House to ratify the treaty, virtually without any reservation, would go to the Assembly and themselves be the leaders of a movement to have Article X struck out. That Article is the backbone of the whole thing; as has been stated, it is the enacting clause of the Covenant. There are no other clauses that call for armaments or anything of that kind; this is the clause that provides for such matters. If it were aggressive in character, if it called for any sort of aggression towards any nations outside of the League, then I could understand why we might be diffident about adopting it; but any one who reads the treaty must know very well that the whole treaty deals with questions of trouble not only as between different members of the League themselves, but also between members of the League and outside nations, and provides that every resource shall be exhausted before Article X can be invoked and war declared. The question has arisen as to the advisability of nations, which are going to send delegates to the League, sending representative delegates instead of delegates appointed by the central government. That question has been raised in all countries except, possibly, Great Britain and Canada. It is suggested that Parliament might elect its delegates to go to the League of Nations and that those delegates should be representative of all parties in the legislative body. I advance that proposition, and possibly it may receive some attention from the members of this House before we take further steps in this matter.	I	repeat,	I am
sorry that our delegates took a stand against Article X. They have given encouragement to those people who are opposed to the British Empire and to France. We all know who in the United States are holding meetings against Article X, and who are tramping upon the British flag in that country to-day. They are not the real Americans; they are not the Americans who were in the war. There are millions of soldiers in the United States to-day who went to the war, and I have yet to hear of one of them who did not speak in the highest terms of Great Britain and her Dominions; and those Americans are the backbone of the friendly portion of the people of the United States. Now, this is the only opportunity we may have for some time of discussing this subject. I trust there may be

some other occasion on which the question will come up, and when that occasion arises, I think our delegates to the League should explain their position somewhat more clearly, if they are going to return to a meeting of the League. Their position on Article X should he considered hy the House and some explanation he given by our delegates.
